en: Now begins the tenth chapter:

The three twice-born castes, remaining steadfast in their own duties, may study [the Veda]; however, it is the settled rule that among them, only the Brāhmaṇa may expound it, and not the other two. 10.1.

"The entire Veda, along with its secret portions, must be mastered by the twice-born" (MDh 2.165): thus the injunction for self-study (*svādhyāya*) is stated for the purpose of acquisition for those of the three higher castes. Furthermore, the non-forgetting of what has been acquired is also enjoined for members of all stages of life (*āśrama*): "One should be constantly devoted to self-study" (MDh 3.65), and likewise, "One should constantly study the scriptures" (MDh 4.19). By its primary function of instructing, and because it sets forth injunctions not known through other means of knowledge, the Veda alone is the "scripture" (*śāstra*). That alone is the scripture; elsewhere, the word "scripture" is used for other works due to a commonality of being a literary composition. Similarly, [it is said]: "Restrained, one should practice the Veda" (MDh 6.95), and "Neglecting the Veda and reviling the Veda" (MDh 11.55). As for the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), that is accomplished by reciting even a single hymn (*sūkta*), a chant (*sāman*), a section (*anuvāka*), a chapter (*khaṇḍa*), or a single verse (*kāṇḍikā*) throughout one's life. It does not imply the constant recollection of the Veda. Thus, since this injunction would otherwise have no scope, it serves merely as a restatement (*anuvāda*).

The statement that "the Brāhmaṇa alone should teach them, not the other two" is intended to exclude the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya from the act of teaching. Now, one might object: since it has been stated that "teaching belongs to the Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 1.88), etc., teaching is already precluded for those two classes anyway. This is not a valid objection; because the performance of a livelihood is explicitly mentioned [in the preceding verse], the prohibition is understood to apply specifically to that purpose. However, this [verse] removes the doubt that the gift of knowledge for the sake of dharma is indeed permitted even for those two.

Now, if there is a general prohibition [of mixed castes], then this is stated as already established for the purpose of generating the occasion for defining the *jñāti* relationship. And by doing so, the connection to be enumerated will not be lost, as in: "The conduct toward Vaiśyas and Śūdras, and the origin of those of mixed castes" (MDh 1.116).

Someone says: "Teaching (*adhyāpana*) is the instruction in the pronunciation of words, whereas exposition (*pravacana*) is also the explanation of their meaning. Therefore, because they are distinct, the cessation of teaching does not entail the cessation of the explanation of its meaning; hence, there is a separate mention [of exposition]. But is it not the case that the word "Veda" does not appear here? From what, then, could the status of being its object (*karmatā*) derive for the act of studying? Or perhaps this "studying" is said to refer even to worldly prose and verse?

It is said: [5] If that were so, the injunction would have an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*). Consequently, there would follow the assumption of a qualification (*adhikāra*) and the assumption of a fundamental basis (*mūlakalpanā*). However, as it has been explained, since this traditional text (*smṛti*) has its basis in perception, there is no contingency of assuming an unseen basis.

Since "the twice-born" (*dvijātayaḥ*) is already established, the phrase "the three castes" (*trayo varṇāḥ*) is for the sake of completing the meter. The same applies to the phrase "established in their own duties" (*svakarmasthāḥ*). || 10.1 ||
A Brāhmaṇa should know the means of livelihood for all [classes] according to the rule;
he should declare them to the others and should himself likewise abide by them. (10.2)

Regarding the statement, “And one should not teach him the Dharma” (MDh 4.80), it was said that no instruction on the Dharma should be given to a Śūdra. This [next rule] is an exception to that, stating that the duties pertaining to his livelihood (*vṛttidharma*) should be taught. Livelihood means the maintenance of one's body and family; one should know the means for that purpose. The phrase “he should declare them to all others” uses the plural number to include the Śūdra. And he himself should likewise be so. The meaning is that the rules of conduct regarding livelihood, having been thus taught, are to be practiced. || 10.2 ||
Due to his distinctiveness, the excellence of his origin, his adherence to the rules of discipline, and the particularity of his refinement, the Brāhmaṇa is the lord of the social orders. 10.3.
But what is the reason that only the brahmin is authorized by virtue of being the subject under discussion, and not the kṣatriyas and others as well?

Because this [preceding statement] is a recommendation based on its being a supplement [to the preceding], he recites it. The meaning is "due to distinction," that is to say, "due to a superiority of qualities. He now states that very superiority: "because of the excellence of his origin (*prakṛtiśraiṣṭhyāt*). This is said because he was born from the highest limb [of the Creator]. "Origin" (*prakṛti*) means the cause. And "because of the observance of the restrictive rule" (*niyamasya ca dhāraṇāt*) refers to the prohibition against drinking intoxicants; this alone is the intended restrictive rule. Or, the observances of a *snātaka*, such as carrying a bamboo staff and so forth, belong to the Brāhmaṇa alone. Furthermore, by "distinction of refinement" (*saṃskārasya ca viśeṣaḥ*), the restrictive rule is intended, as are the *snātaka* observances, based on such passages as "with [mantras] reaching the heart" (VaDh 3.31); or else, because initiation (*upanayana*) and the like are prescribed for the child alone, whereas for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya they occur at ages eleven and twelve respectively, once childhood has passed. For this reason, among the social classes (*varṇas*), the Brāhmaṇa is the lord and the ruler. 10.3.
What, then, are these so-called *varṇas*? Is the word *varṇa* a term denoting human species? No, he says:
"The Brāhmaṇa, the Kṣatriya, and the Vaiśya are the three twice-born *varṇas*;
the fourth is the once-born Śūdra, but there is no fifth. (10.4)

There are four castes (*varṇas*), beginning with the Brāhmaṇas and ending with the Śūdras. Others, however, such as the Barbaras, Kaivartas, and so forth, are of mixed origin (*saṃkīrṇayoni*), as will be explained later. Among these, three of the four are twice-born (*dvijāti*), because for them the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) is prescribed. The Śūdra is once-born (*ekajāti*). For him there is no initiation, because the injunction for initiation specifies particular castes, such as: "One should initiate a Brāhmaṇa in the eighth year, a Kṣatriya in the eleventh, and a Vaiśya in the twelfth. They do not mention the Śūdra at any time [in this context].

Now, one might object: "Since no specific time is mentioned, let the initiation (*upanayana*) of a Śūdra be performed at an indefinite time. This would be the case if the originative injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*) for initiation were stated in general terms without being connected to specific [castes]. However, these [passages] which mention specific castes and times are merely commendatory statements (*stuti*) intended to provide a reason (*nimitta*). There is no separate originative injunction for it. Therefore, on the strength of what authority could its initiation be performed at an indefinite time?
If this is so, then what is the purpose of the statement, "In the fourth [birth], he is once-born"?

True. This is for the purpose of dispelling a mere suspicion. The phrase "it is not faulty except when accompanied by mantras" (MDh 10.127) raises the possibility that eating at an unregulated time without mantras might be permitted;
however, since this statement occurs within the section on *pākayajña* rites, and because it is heard in close proximity to them, its purpose is fulfilled there and it cannot apply elsewhere.
For this very reason, it was stated that this is merely a [dispelling of] suspicion.
But from the perspective of ultimate truth, the tenth verse [10.4] is intended for the purpose of establishing the rules of conventional usage.
Among wives of equal caste from all social classes whose wombs have not been violated, those born in the direct order [of castes] are to be known as belonging to that same caste. 10.5.

Furthermore, what indeed are these so-called "Brāhmaṇas" and the rest? For their mutual distinction cannot be ascertained. Since universals (jāti) are apprehended dependent upon individuals (vyakti), and since individuals are incapable of making known the distinction between those [universals] without the apprehension of a specific configuration of their own parts, [the distinction remains unestablished]. Nor is there a difference in vocal form among Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and others, such that they would be perceptible by sight through the inherence of a [visible] form, as is the case with cows and horses. Nor are they objects of other activities through a distinction in smell, taste, and so forth, like melted ghee or oil. Nor can their distinction be determined by properties such as purity of conduct or tawny hair, because such traits are observed to be intermingled everywhere. Furthermore, social convention depends upon persons; and since persons are prone to much deception, the reality of the matter is not established in the end.

Therefore, the definition of caste (*jāti*) is stated: this is the characteristic of caste among all social classes (*varṇa*), namely, that those born of wives who are of equal status—meaning they are of the same caste and have been duly wedded—are to be known by that very caste. Generally, whatever the caste of the parents may be, that same caste is to be understood for the offspring born of a wedded wife. Because the term "wife" (*patnī*) is a relative word, the husband is understood from its mention; thus, he by whom she was wedded is obtained as the father. Consequently, one who is born of her by that very person by whom she was wedded is then of that same caste.

Furthermore, the inclusion of the term "one whose womb is unviolated" (akṣatayoni) excludes those who might be suspected of attaining the status of a wife through the sacrament of remarriage, as well as the mothers of the *sahoḍha* and *kānīna* sons.

But is it not the case that these women have no marriage sacrament (*vivāhasaṃskāra*) at all, because of the statement: “The mantras for taking the hand apply to maidens” (MDh 8.226)? Even though there is the mention of marriage in the rule, “That embryo belongs to the one who marries her” (MDh 9.173), this does not constitute a recognition of a scriptural sacrament, because that statement merely expresses a possibility (*prāptimātra*) and is not a mandatory injunction. Therefore, the verbal root [in *voḍhuḥ*] signifies mere acceptance; the meaning is “of the one who accepts. She belongs to whoever has accepted her by deceiving the father and others, and consequently, the son belongs to him as well, since there is no sacrament for a remarried woman (*punarbhū*). This is what is meant by the reading: “If she should be one whose womb is unviolated” (MDh 9.176). Even in the case of a woman who has returned after having left, the word “again” (*punaḥ*) serves as a marker of recognition, and thus they are said to belong to the husband. Yet, there is no entitlement to perform rites together with such women; the term *patnī* (wife) applies only in connection with sacrificial acts. Consequently, the word *akṣatayoni* (unviolated womb) is redundant here. Regarding this, earlier commentators read *nārīṣu* (among women) as a synonym for *patnī*; but even that is of no consequence. For if only the word *akṣatayoni* were used, those born of women who have not undergone the sacraments would also be considered of that same caste. By the inclusion of the word *patnī*, which refers to one who has been consecrated by scriptural rite and brought to the status of a wife, she alone is understood. As for those who are approached while still virgins, they may indeed be *akṣatayoni*, but they are not *patnīs*. Therefore, the purpose of the term *akṣatayoni* must be stated.

It is replied: As for what was stated, that "they are not wives because of the absence of connection with a sacrifice," if they were to be married, that very act would constitute a sacrifice. Furthermore, in those cases as well, there is indeed a sacrifice involving Pūṣan, Varuṇa, and Aryaman. The words *yāga* and *yajña* have the same meaning. Therefore, they should indeed be wives. It is only logical that they are not wives precisely because, being non-maidens, they are not eligible for marriage.

Therefore, even if [the term] were meaningless, the purpose of the word *akṣatayoni* (one whose womb is unviolated) is stated. It is observed in common usage that the word *patnī* (wife) is employed by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) even when there is no connection to a sacrifice, as in "the wife of a washerman. Just as elsewhere, the word *gṛhiṇī* (housewife) is used for women who are kept in confinement; that too is used there for a woman in the primary sense of "wife" due to some similarity of attributes. Although metaphorical indication is not logical when the primary sense is available, nevertheless, acting as a friend to those of dull intellect, he dispels a mere suspicion. For what indeed is not suspected by those of deluded minds?

The inclusion of the term *ānulomya* ("in accordance with") is for the sake of what follows. Even for those who read the text as "those very [words]," the meaning is the same: that they belong to that same class (*tajjātīya*). To this it is replied: What is the basis of authority for this recollection of the authors of the *Smṛtis*? Since it does not have the nature of a performed action, it is not equal to the instruction on *dharma* and *adharma*. Furthermore, it has been stated that there is no other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) [for it]. If another *Smṛti* were its source, it would result in a "blind tradition," as shown in the verse on the means of valid cognition (cf. MDh 2.6). It is said in reply: Its basis is simply the usage of the elders (*vṛddhavyavahāra*), just like the *Smṛti* concerning grammatical correctness (*sādhutva*).
But has it not been said that this [tradition] is subject to error?

Precisely for that reason, the restrictive Smṛtis are fruitful. It cannot be asserted that the recollection of those who are learned is otherwise; those established in the Śāstras are more authoritative. Furthermore, it is possible that their root is an beginningless practice. According to the view of some, even direct perception is possible for those refined by these Smṛtis and whose noble lineage and caste are well-known. This has been explained in detail in the *Smṛtiviveka*.
But is it not the case that in another Smṛti there is no such distinction?
For it says: "From men of the same caste, upon women of the same caste, are born those of the same lineage; through marriages not censured, sons are born who increase the progeny. (YDh 1.89)

By the first half [of the verse], caste (*jāti*) is indicated; by the latter, the capacity for the increase of progeny among those born of the *brāhma* and other forms of marriage is shown. Regarding that [first half], in the phrase "from those of the same class (*savarṇa*) upon women of the same class," the word "wife" (*patnī*) does not occur.

How is it that it does not occur? For it has been stated: "This rule is ordained for married women" (YDh 1.92). Or rather, let it not be so; a specific Smṛti rule is stronger than a general one. Perception is stronger than non-perception, because it is possible that a distinction was not seen by one [author] but was seen by another.
Therefore, the tradition of those who are learned (*abhiyukta*) is authoritative because it possesses a possible basis.

But is this not a non-definition because it lacks pervasion (*avyāpti*)? For by this [definition], the Brahminhood of the *sahoḍha*, the *kānīna*, the *paunarbhava*, and so forth, would not be established. If you argue that "the Brahminhood of the *kuṇḍa*, the *golaka*, and the *kṣetraja* is indeed unintended for them," then what is their caste? Furthermore, if the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* lack Brahminhood, the prohibition [against them] at a *śrāddha* ceremony would be purposeless since they have no entitlement there, and it would contradict other Smṛtis.
"This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste. (YDh 2.137)

Furthermore, that which is the definition (*lakṣaṇa*) is itself the thing defined (*lakṣya*). The thing defined is that which is not yet known, while the definition is that which is already known. For example, when there is doubt as to who Devadatta is, one says: "He is the one with the armlet, the earring, the broad chest, and the rounded arms. But here, it would be just like if someone were asked, "What is a crow? and the answer given were, "That which is born from a crow"; or if asked, "Who is a Brāhmaṇa?", the answer were, "He who is born from a Brāhmaṇa. For even in the case of the progenitor, Brāhmaṇahood is not established, and this contradicts logic. In the world, that which is born from a male of the same species by a female of the same species becomes of that same species; for example, a cow from a cow is a cow, and a horse from a mare is a horse. To this it is replied: As for what was said—"What is their caste?"—what need is there for another caste? They are, first of all, human beings. And they are entitled to perform the duties of men, even without having acquired a specific caste distinction, on account of being sons and through rites such as the *śrāddha*. Furthermore, all are entitled to the act of giving.

But surely, without the teaching of a specific distinction, linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) cannot be established, because the human genus (*manuṣyajāti*) is common to all. This is not so; for every individual possesses their own particular name, such as Devadatta or Yajñadatta. If it is argued that a designation based on relationship must be made, then they are designated as "born of an unmarried woman" (*kānīna*) or "born of a pregnant bride" (*sahoḍha*). If it is further argued that since these [terms] also exist among the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), they are merely general in form, then the designation will be made by means of the progenitor, such as "the *kānīna* son of Devadatta. Therefore, the objection as to how the designation is possible is irrelevant.

If that is so, then all dharmas indeed apply to the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), as stated in Manu Smṛti 1.2: “and for those born in the intermediate [orders]” (*antaraprabhavānām*). In this context, the plurality refers to the scope of the four castes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa. Nor is there a single caste even among these, because this definition applies to all castes. Just as one born to a Brāhmaṇa father from a Brāhmaṇī mother who has been wedded by him is a Brāhmaṇa, so too are the Kṣatriyas and others born from mothers and fathers of the same caste. And in the absence of all particular instances (*viśeṣa*), how could there be a universal (*sāmānya*)? For indeed, in the absence of all particular instances such as the *śiṃśapā* tree, the existence of the universal "treeness" (*vṛkṣatva*) is impossible.

And those born in between [the castes] are of both *anuloma* (direct) and *pratiloma* (inverse) origin. Among them, the *anulomas* belong to the caste of their mother, while the *pratilomas* are "devoid of dharma" (GDh 4.25), except for [the duties of] non-violence and so forth. And all of them have been specifically designated by their own respective names. Yet, not even the name of these [intermediate castes] exists there [in the Veda]. In that case, what are those dharmas by which they would be authorized? And where is that scriptural statement which would authorize them? For there is no rule of dharma based on a specific caste, because the scripture authorizes both the members of all four *varṇas* and those born in between.

It is said in reply: First, as for the mention of the four *varṇas* in connection with non-violence and other duties (*ahiṃsādi*) [cf. MDh 10.63], that is intended merely as an illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*) of human beings in general. This is because, even though there is an entitlement for those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), the term must function in its primary sense; on the contrary, it is capable of indicating the other castes associated with them, and cannot remain restricted to those intermediate states alone. We shall explain this very point at MDh 10.63. Furthermore, there is this statement: "All those born of illicit unions (*apadhvaṃsa*) are declared to share the same *dharma* as Śūdras" (MDh 10.41). *Apadhvaṃsa* means the absence of sacramental rites (*asaṃskāra*). That is of eight kinds, as stated in the passage beginning with "by the transgression of the castes" (MDh 10.24). Transgression (*vyabhicāra*) consists in approaching the wives of others or women of one's own caste. We shall discuss the rest later. Therefore, even though they do not possess the status of a *varṇa*, their entitlement is based solely on scriptural injunction (*vācanika*).

But for a Kṣatriya, there is indeed the status of belonging to the mother’s caste (*mātṛjātīyatva*), because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). A specific duty is heard in the text: "The son of a *dvyāmuṣyāyaṇa* [belongs to both] due to the agreement. Furthermore, in other Śrauta texts, a different rule regarding him is seen. Therefore, he belongs to the same caste as the Brāhmaṇa and others, and shares an equal portion with his paternal uncle, according to the rule: "Therefore, one should honor him according to the law" (MDh 9.121). And that [equal share] is not appropriate under the rule as previously stated; for in that case, he would have the status of a Śūdra. Since it has been stated that wealth is for the purpose of sacrifice, how could such a person receive a share? The *Kuṇḍa* and *Golaka* are indeed *kṣetraja* sons. The practice of the learned (*śiṣṭasamācāra*) is exactly like this: Pāṇḍu, Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and Vidura, being *kṣetraja* sons, belong to the caste of their mothers. Hence, the prohibition against them at the *śrāddha* ceremony is logical. Moreover, even an outcast (*patita*) is prohibited therein, since he is excluded from all religious duties (*dharma*) and thus there is no possibility of his entitlement [to a share] arising. As for the other Smṛti text stating "among those of the same caste" (YDh 2.137), that should be explained as a restatement of what has already been said, applicable according to the circumstances, or as referring specifically to the *kāryaputra*.

And as for that characteristic which is well-known, is it not the case that the meaning of "brāhmaṇa" is not at all established by worldly convention? Wherever the word "brāhmaṇa" and so forth is employed, the statement is intended to exclude the application of other [erroneous] designations. This very thing is the defining characteristic of caste (*jāti*) with respect to one's mother and father; nor is there an infinite regress, because *saṃsāra* is beginningless.

However, there would be a direct contradiction with the principle under discussion if these *jātis* were accessible through direct perception (*vyavasāya*). Rather, they must exist as characterized by memory (*smṛti*), according to how they are remembered. Or, for example, words such as "Vasiṣṭha" are employed in reference to objects known through an uninterrupted tradition of memory, even without a perceived common property (*anvayadharma*), and they serve as the basis for linguistic usage, as in "The Brāhmaṇas of Vasiṣṭha" or "O sons of Vasiṣṭha, listen! This should be understood in the same way. Just as, while Brāhmaṇahood is common to all, specific distinctions such as "Bhṛgus," "Vatsas," or "Bhāradvājas" are established solely on the authority of tradition (*smṛti*), so too, while humanity is common to all, the linguistic usage distinguishing "these are Brāhmaṇas" from "these are Kṣatriyas" and so forth is logically justified.

Furthermore, those who cite the *Jābāla* Śruti as evidence for [the validity of the signs of caste] state: "Satyakāma Jābāla asked his mother, 'What is my lineage? She replied to him thus: 'In my youth, while I was a maidservant wandering about much, I conceived you. I do not know that [your lineage]. Having heard this, he went to Hāridrumata Gautama. He said to him: 'I wish to live with you as a religious student (*brahmacarya*). He said to him: 'Of what lineage are you? He replied: 'I asked my mother, and my mother replied, "In my youth... and so forth. Gautama said: 'One who is not a Brahmin would not be able to speak such a truth. My dear, bring the fuel; I shall initiate you' (ChU 4.4.1–5). The meaning of this is as follows: "In my youth, I had sexual union with many men; I do not know by whom you were begotten. Gautama, however, determined from her truthful speech that he was born of a Brahmin, and thereupon initiated him. Therefore, we consider that even among women who have been promiscuous but are unmarried, children born of a man of the same caste belong to that same caste.

This is of no consequence, because I took you [in marriage] during my youth. Indeed, in youth, memory does not become firm, owing to the abundance of longing in the mind during youth. Furthermore, as a female attendant, I was wandering about much for the sake of serving, being afflicted by hunger and not remaining in one place; therefore, I have no recollection of my husband’s clan name.

Therefore, this is established: those born of a wife married to a man of the same caste are of that same caste. Even for Gautama, the understanding that "this man is a Brāhmaṇa" does not arise from that statement [of his]; rather, he already knows him to be a Brāhmaṇa beforehand. He merely does not know his *gotra*. The inquiry regarding the *gotra* should be understood as an inquiry regarding the *caraṇa* (Vedic school). In that regard, there is a distinction in the initiation (*upanayana*). However, the purpose of the initiation is not served by the distinction of *gotra*. It is not as some say: "This is an inquiry into caste (*jāti*) because of noble birth; through the *gotra*, I shall understand the caste. For if there were a direct inquiry into caste, it would be mere loquacity. (10.5)
Sons begotten by the twice-born upon women born immediately after them in the social order are said to be equal [to their fathers], yet they are censured due to the defect of their mothers. (10.6)

Those sons who are born in the direct order (*ānulomya*) from women immediately following [the father's caste] without any interval are to be known as *sadṛśa* (similar), but not as belonging to that same caste (*tajjātīya*). For example, [a son born] to a Kṣatriya woman from a Brāhmaṇa, or to a Vaiśya woman from a Kṣatriya. They are similar to them, but not "identical to them" (MDh 10.5). The reason for this is: "they are censured due to the defect of the mother. Because of the mention of "similarity," they are superior to the mother but inferior to the father. Since the plural number is used in the word "by the twice-born" (*dvijaiḥ*) and the defect of the mother is specifically mentioned, this applies only to those born in the direct order (*ānulomya*). In the inverse order (*prātilomya*), because the status is determined by the father, the son belongs to a caste lower than the mother’s, being inferior even to the father. Therefore, the mention of "direct order" in the preceding verse—which was stated to be "for the sake of what follows"—is redundant here; it is, however, taught again in the subsequent verses. (10.6)
This is the eternal rule for those born of women one degree lower;
one should know this righteous rule to apply to those born of women two or three degrees lower. (10.7)

He restates the meaning expressed by the first half-verse; by the second, he provides a summary of what is to be said. "Separated by two or one": for a Brāhmaṇa, a Śūdra woman is separated by two [classes], and a Vaiśya woman is separated by one. This verse is not particularly purposeful. (10.7)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of a Vaiśya is born one named Ambaṣṭha;
from the daughter of a Śūdra is born a Niṣāda, who is called a Pāraśava. (10.8)

A Vaiśya woman is one degree removed from a Brāhmaṇa; the son born of her is an Ambaṣṭha. In another Smṛti, he is called a Bhṛjjakaṇṭha (GDh 4.20). From a Śūdra girl who is two degrees removed, there is a Niṣāda and a Pāraśava. They explain that the word *niṣāda* also applies to those of the pratiloma castes. They state that the mention of the word "girl" (*kanyā*) is intended to indicate any woman in general. The meaning is "from a Vaiśya woman"; this should be understood in all similar cases. (10.8)
From a Kṣatriya man and a Śūdra woman is born a creature named Ugra, who possesses the physical form of both a Kṣatriya and a Śūdra and whose conduct and pastimes are cruel. (10.9)

Conduct and deportment consist of bodily movement and vocal activity; these two become cruel in him. This is a restatement of his inherent nature. The word *vapuḥ* (body) indeed signifies innate disposition (*svabhāva*). Because he is born from both [lineages], he possesses the characteristics of both. || 10.9 ||
For a Brāhmaṇa, [sons born] from women of the three castes; for a Kṣatriya, from women of two castes; and for a Vaiśya, from one caste—these six are recorded as apasadas.

In this context, the first three quarters [of the verse] are merely a restatement; the fourth quarter, however, is intended to designate the *apasadās* (outcastes). These should be understood as the *apasadās* born from women one or two degrees lower than the men of the three *varṇas*. They are called *apasadās* because they have fallen away (*avasannāḥ*) from the fruit that is the purpose of a son; they are censured in comparison with sons of the same caste. (10.10)
From a Kṣatriya father and a Brāhmaṇa maiden, a Sūta is born by birth;
from a Vaiśya father, the Māgadha and the Vaideha are born as the sons of a royal and a Brāhmaṇa woman respectively.

The previous rule applies to the natural order; however, this [following rule] is stated for the inverse order. The mention of "maiden" has already been explained (cf. 10.8). From Vaiśyas, by respective order, come the Māgadha and the Vaideha: the Māgadha from a Kṣatriya woman and the Vaideha from a Brāhmaṇa woman. 10.11.
From a Śūdra, on women of the Vaiśya, Rājanya, and Brāhmaṇa castes, are born the Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest among men—through the intermixture of the castes. (10.12)

Here too, the correspondence is strictly according to the order of enumeration. Although the designation "vaiśyarājanya" refers to the genus (*jāti*), the feminine gender is understood by implication, as in the cases of "deer's milk" (*mṛgakṣīram*) and "hen's egg" (*kukkuṭāṇḍam*). The feminine suffix was not employed here merely for the sake of metrical convenience. || 10.12 ||
But when there is an interval of one caste [between parents], they are born in the natural order as the Ambaṣṭha and the Ugra, as recorded in tradition;
likewise, the Kṣattṛ and the Vaidehaka are born in the inverse order.

From a Brāhmaṇa on a Vaiśya woman one step removed in caste, an Ambaṣṭha is born; from a Kṣatriya on a Śūdra woman, an Ugra is born. These two are born in the natural order (ānulomya). Likewise, in the inverse order (prātilomya), from a Śūdra on a Kṣatriya woman a Kṣattṛ is born, and from a Vaiśya on a Brāhmaṇa woman a Vaideha is born. These two are equal in activities such as building houses and the like, but not in sacrifices and other such rites. The Caṇḍāla alone is born in the inverse order and is untouchable; as stated in the verse regarding the Divākīrti, bathing occurs upon touching him alone, and not upon touching other inverse-born castes. For the Sūta, Māgadha, and Āyogava, who are born from immediate unions, their status as untouchables is established by the maxim of the "stick and the cake" (daṇḍāpūpikā), just like that of the Caṇḍāla. || 10.13 ||
Those sons of the twice-born who are born of women immediately following [the wife of the same caste], as described in order,
are designated by the name "anantara" (immediate) due to the defect of their mothers.

Just as [the offspring] of a Brāhmaṇa from a Kṣatriya woman and a Vaiśya woman [are designated], so too [the offspring] of a Kṣatriya from both [of these two classes] are designated by the name "Anantara. Anantara means an *anuloma* caste; the meaning is that they belong to the same caste as their mother. The use of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) is not intended to be restrictive. For this very reason, he says, "due to the defect of the mother. They are not defiled by the superiority of the father's caste. And thus, even though there is a mixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*), by virtue of the scriptural statement, they are recorded as belonging to the mother's caste. What is meant is that the sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*) must be performed for them. Indeed, without this scriptural statement, the sacramental rites of a Kṣatriya and so forth would not be applicable to them, because they would be a distinct caste, like a mule (*aśvatara*). But since the mother's caste is declared by the scriptural statement, there is no fault. (10.14)
From a Brāhmaṇa and the daughter of an Ugra is born one named Āvṛta; from the daughter of an Ambaṣṭha is born an Ābhīra, but from the daughter of an Āyogava is born a Dhigvaṇa. (10.15)
The Āyogava, the Kṣattṛ, and the Caṇḍāla—the lowest of men—these three base-born (apasada) sons are born from a Śūdra woman through men of the higher castes in the reverse order. 10.16.
From a Vaiśya are born the Māgadha and the Vaideha; from a Kṣatriya, however, is born the Sūta alone.
These others are also three base-born (apasada) castes who are produced in the reverse order.
One born from a Niṣāda father and a Śūdra mother is by birth a Pukkasa;
but one born from a Śūdra father and a Niṣāda mother is known as a Kukkuṭaka. || 10.18 ||

This Niṣāda mentioned in this verse is not the one born from a Śūdra woman and a Brāhmaṇa who was previously mentioned. What then? It is the one born in the inverse order (pratiloma) who will be described hereafter; for, since the context concerns those born in the inverse order, the Niṣāda caste is well known as being born from a Pulkasa woman. Likewise, from a Śūdra man and a Niṣāda woman, a Kukkuṭaka is born. (10.18)
One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is known as a Śvapāka;
one produced by a Vaidehaka father and an Ambaṣṭhī mother is called a Veṇa.

Women are born in the natural order (anuloma), while men are born in the inverse order (pratiloma); when these two unite, the offspring are of the inverse castes (pratilomajāti), namely the Śvapāka and the Veṇa. || 10.19 ||
Those whom twice-born men beget on wives of equal caste, but who are devoid of the sacred observances and excluded from the Sāvitrī, one should designate as Vrātyas. (10.20)

These are not *varṇasaṃkara*s born in the inverse order; therefore, they are mentioned in this rule. Those whom the twice-born beget on women of their own caste, yet who lack Vedic vows, are non-students (*abrahmacārin*), have fallen away from the *Sāvitrī*, and are devoid of initiation (*upanayana*)—they should then be designated as *vrātyas*. The construction is not "those who beget the vowless"; for neither those who possess vows nor those who are vowless beget [the children], since the rite of initiation is prescribed for those already born. This is a restatement of the characteristics of the *vrātya* already mentioned, intended to introduce what follows. As for the reading: "Those whom they beget on a woman without vows, one should designate them as *vrātyas*," that is incorrect, because it contradicts the previously stated definition of a *vrātya*. (10.20)
From a Vrātya Brahmin is born the evil-natured Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka,
as well as the Āvantya, the Vāṭadhāna, the Puṣpadha, and the Śaikha.

The phrase “among women of their own caste” (*svavarṇāsu*) is carried over from the preceding verse, because the female sex is not explicitly mentioned here and because there is a necessary dependence upon it. In another *Smṛti*, one born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Vaiśya woman is recorded as a *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka*. Therefore, he qualifies [the subject] as “of evil nature” (*pāpātman*); for that [other type] is not of evil nature due to being born in the natural order (*anuloma*). And since this one is born from a *vrātya* who is himself unrefined in soul (*asaṃskṛtātman*), it is appropriate that he is censured because of his lack of qualification [for sacraments]. Furthermore, these are not merely synonymous terms, as their usage differs according to regional conventions.

But it has been explained by the predecessors: these are the names of his sons and grandsons. Bhṛjjakaṇṭaka was born of a Brāhmaṇī woman; Āvantya was born of an Āvantī woman; in that same lineage was Vāṭadhāna; from Vāṭadhāna came Puṣpaśekhara; and so it continues for the subsequent generations as well. 10.21.
From a Vratya of the Rajanya caste are born the Jhalla, the Malla, and the Licchivi;
as well as the Nata, the Karana, the Khasa, and the Dravidian.
From a Vrātya Vaiśya are born the Sudhanvan, the Ācārya, the Kāruṣa,
the Vijanman, the Maitra, and the Sātvata.
It should be understood that those of such a kind are well-known by these very designations. 10.22–23.
Through adultery, through the knowing of women who should not be known, and through the abandonment of one's own duties, the intermixture of castes arises. (10.24)

Adultery is sexual intercourse with the wife of another. That [occurs] with women of the same caste who belong to others—whether married or unmarried, and whether born in the natural (anuloma) or inverse (pratiloma) order—and with one's own [wife] when she is not permitted. "Sexual intercourse with those who should not be approached" (*avedyāvedana*) means marrying those who should not be married. Those who should not be married include sisters, nieces, and so forth; likewise, those who are not of the [proper] womb (*ayoni*). The abandonment of one's own duties refers to the neglect of such acts as the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and the study of the Vedas. Some maintain that even the occupations of warriors (*kṣatriya*) and others are thus described as [abandoning one's own duties] when they are inherited by sons and grandsons. (10.24)
But those of mixed origin who are born from inverse and natural unions,
and those who are mutually intermingled— I shall describe them in their entirety.

*Vyatiṣaṅga* means connection. It refers to the mutual intermingling of those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) with others of the natural order as well as the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and likewise of those born in the inverse order with others of the inverse order as well as the natural order. This statement is for the purpose of providing the technical designations that will be explained hereafter. (10.25)
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Caṇḍāla, the lowest of men;
the Māgadha, the Kṣattṛ caste, and likewise the Āyogava. (10.26)
These, whose characteristics have already been stated, are presented again in reverse order for the sake of what follows. 10.26.
These six produce offspring of similar caste within their own wombs; however, they also procreate children belonging to the mother's caste when united with women of superior castes. (10.27)

These *sūtas* and others born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) produce offspring similar to themselves when they procreate within their own wombs; that is to say, they produce those belonging to their own caste. For example: a *sūta* begets a *sūta* upon a *sūtā*; likewise, a *caṇḍāla* begets a *caṇḍāla* upon a *caṇḍālā*. Furthermore, those who are born according to the mother’s caste—the *anulomas* previously mentioned as "those [born of women] of the next lower caste" (*tān anantarānāmnaḥ*, MDh 10.14)—they too produce only similar offspring within their own wombs. For instance, an *ambaṣṭha* begets an *ambaṣṭha* upon an *ambaṣṭhā*. Similarly, those who are inferior to the Vaiśya beget Vaiśyas upon a Vaiśya woman, because it has been stated that they possess the mother’s caste.

Others, however, read: "They procreate within the mother's caste. And this is the meaning: in their own wombs—such as the Ambaṣṭha and others—and within the mother's caste, namely the Vaiśya woman, they beget offspring who are indeed similar [to themselves]. Although the Ambaṣṭhas and others are superior to pure Vaiśyas, they are nevertheless said to be equal, because both groups have the right to the duties of a Vaiśya.

The inclusion of the term *anuloma* (in the same order) is obtained through the force of the word *mātṛjāti* (of the mother’s caste), even though [the preceding verse] refers back to the natural (*prakṛti*) inverse order as well. It should be understood that those who approach women of higher castes in the inverse order produce offspring that are even more degraded; this is to be known from a consideration of what is about to be stated. For those born of women of their own caste by Āyogavas and others do not receive the designation of "Āyogava" and so forth. However, the mention of "similar" [offspring] is based on the commonality of being born in the inverse order. And the state of being "more degraded" is employed without regard for internal distinctions. Therefore, the meaning of the sentence here is this: from those born in the inverse order, whether toward women of the same caste or toward women of superior castes, they remain indeed of the inverse order. (10.27)
Just as for the three castes, a son is born from two [members] of one's own self,
so too, by immediate succession, is it among the outsiders according to their respective orders.

The self of this Brāhmaṇa is born from the three castes. In the two castes of the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya, the state of being twice-born (*dvijatva*) arises; likewise, [it arises] in his own womb. Thus, the Brāhmaṇa produces twice-born men from the three castes. Similarly, even among those outside [the pale], by inverse order (*prātilomya*), the self of the Kṣatriya and the Brāhmaṇa becomes twice-born through the Vaiśya and the Kṣatriya respectively. And once the state of being twice-born exists, the initiation (*upanayana*) must be performed. And he will say: "These six possess the duties of the twice-born" (MDh 10.41). But this much is the distinction: those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) are "of the mother's caste" (10.27), meaning they belong to the same caste as their mother. We shall explain later that this is merely a figurative praise (10.28).
And they also procreate upon the wives of others many outsiders, even more corrupted than themselves, who are held in contempt by one another. (10.29)

And those six, beginning with the Āyogava, also procreate many further outsiders among one another's wives. For example: the Āyogava begets upon the wife of a Kṣattṛ, and the Kṣattṛ upon an Āyogavī; thus they mutually procreate those who are more despised than themselves. For example: the Āyogava begets upon the wife of a Kṣattṛ one even more outside than himself, and one even more outside than that upon a Caṇḍālī. Thus it is in every case. (10.29)
Just as a Śūdra begets an outcaste being upon a Brāhmaṇī woman, so too does an outcaste beget one even more outcaste upon a woman of the four castes. || 10.30 ||

Thus, regarding the intermixture of castes through mutual union, the birth of those who are outside the [fourfold] system has been described according to the previous rule. Now, the fourfold caste system (cāturvarṇya) is being discussed. In this context, the root *sū* is employed as having the same meaning as *jan*, namely "to produce" or "to beget. This is indicated by the following verse. (10.30)
Acting in opposition [to their own kind], those outsiders again procreate even more outsiders—
fifteen distinct castes, indeed, born from the inferior and the most inferior.

For each of the social classes (*varṇa*), however, there are offspring of mixed origin: some are born in the natural order (*anuloma*), some in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and some in both the natural and inverse orders. For the Brāhmaṇa, there are those born in the natural order; for the Śūdra, only those born in the inverse order; and for the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya, there are both those born in the natural order and those born in the inverse order. Specifically, for the Kṣatriya there are two born in the natural order and one born in the inverse order; for the Vaiśya, there is one born in the natural order and two born in the inverse order. Thus, these constitute twelve types of offspring born in the natural and inverse orders. For each of these, when they marry women of the four [classes], four further subdivisions arise. Some of these are inferior (*hīna*) and some are not inferior (*ahīna*); but all of them are indeed more excluded (*bāhyatara*). This "more excluded" status refers to a distance from the caste of their mother and father, due to their inferiority in ritual duties (*karman*). This is now made clear by means of examples.
First, we shall speak of those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*).

An *āyogava* is one born from a *śūdra* father and a *vaiśya* mother; he begets four [sons] in a *śūdra*, a *vaiśya*, a *kṣatriya*, and a *brāhmaṇī* woman. Thus, including himself, this *āyogava* is fivefold. The same applies to the *kṣattṛ* and the *caṇḍāla*. In this way, there are three groups of five from the *śūdra*, making fifteen types in total.

Thus, there are two born from a Vaiśya in the inverse order (*pratiloma*): the Māgadha from a Kṣatriya woman and the Vaidehaka from a Brāhmaṇa woman. [The Āyogava] is born in the direct order (*anuloma*) from a Śūdra woman. In that regard, when one born of a Śūdra woman procreates offspring within the four castes (*cāturvarṇya*), this same pattern applies. When he approaches a Śūdra woman, a lower caste is born in comparison to him; likewise, approaching a Vaiśya woman, he produces an even lower one. Similarly, those born solely from a Śūdra man into Kṣatriya and Brāhmaṇa women are superior. Thus, depending on the relative status, they may be either higher or lower. This should be understood to apply to the Kṣatriya and the Brāhmaṇa as well. However, for the Brāhmaṇa, this is the distinction: his offspring are only in the direct order (*anuloma*).

Thus, there are fifteen subdivisions for each of the four primary castes (*caturvarṇa*), which together amount to sixty; these, together with the four principal castes, constitute the sixty-four. Due to their mutual intermixture, other infinite divisions arise among them. As it has been said: "And they [beget] many more outsiders" (MDh 10.29).

"Acting contrary" means by transgressing the scriptures. "Engaging in sexual union" means copulating. "Low and not low" is a single compound term; or alternatively, being low themselves, they procreate—that is, they give birth to—those who are low. Regarding the phrase "only fifteen castes," since the fifth [caste] lacks the status of a caste according to the rule "but there is no fifth" (MDh 10.4), the status of being a caste among the fifteen should be understood as a figurative designation. 10.31.
From a Dasyu and an Ayogava is born a Sairandhra, who knows how to apply cosmetics and personal adornments, who is not a slave yet lives as one, and who subsists by the trade of a hunter.

*Prasādhana* means adornment. *Upacāra* means attendance. She is one who knows the rules regarding the arrangement of hair, the application of saffron, sandalwood, and other unguents, the massaging of hands and feet, and the proper timing for tasks that must be performed quickly due to the desire for gain; such a person is described thus. She lives as a slave though not a slave by birth (*adāsaṃ dāsyajīvanam*). She serves someone for a year’s wage or a six-month wage. Alternatively, through her knowledge of these rules, she becomes an attendant to all for the sake of her livelihood. Or she follows the profession of a hunter (*vāgurāvṛtti*). This is the second means of subsistence. A *vāgurā* is the killing of wild animals. And this [work] is for the Aryas for the sake of rites for the gods and ancestors, and for the sake of hunger, but not like a hunter who lives by killing animals and selling their meat. Killing many living beings for the sake of a livelihood occurs only by royal command. She gives birth to one named *sairandhra*. A *dasyu* is a specific caste to be mentioned later. By implication, the female gender is understood from the context. (10.32)
The Vaideha, however, procreates the Maitreyaka, who praises men incessantly and strikes a bell at the break of dawn. (10.33)

One born from an *āyogavī* woman is called a *maitreyaka* by name; he produces [this caste]. A *vaidehaka* is one born from a *vaiśya* father and a *brāhmaṇī* mother. There is an alternative reading, "maireyaka. It means "madhūka-like"; this is a term of comparison, because he speaks sweetly like the *madhūka* flower. Alternatively, it is derived from the root *madhukāyati*, with the suffix *ḍa* according to Pāṇini 3.2.101 ("it is seen in other cases as well"), and the lengthening of the vowel according to Pāṇini 6.3.137 ("for others as well"), with the initial vowel-vṛddhi by a suffix denoting the same meaning (*svārthika*). His livelihood is as follows: he constantly and at all times praises men, and is thus called a *bandī*. At the break of dawn, during the time of awakening, he strikes and beats a bell for the purpose of waking kings, lords, and others. He likewise produces [the next caste] from an *āyogavī* woman, because that is the subject under discussion. 10.33.
The Niṣāda begets the Mārgava, a slave who lives by the work of boats;
those dwelling in Āryāvarta call him a Kaivarta.

He who was previously mentioned as the *niṣāda*—born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Śūdra mother in the inverse order—is not the one referred to here; rather, it is the *pratiloma* born from a Dasyu-like woman. He is called Mārgava, born in the inverse order from an Āyogavī woman; he has these two other names: Dāsa and Kaivarta. The region of Āryāvarta is well known. His livelihood: he lives by the work of boats, that is, by rowing boats. (10.34)
Among the Āyogavīs—who wear the clothes of the dead, are ignoble, and eat despised food—these three base-born castes arise separately. (10.35)

The maternal origins of those three who were just described as being at the end of the [list of] paths have not been stated; this verse is for the purpose of explaining them. These [beings] are born of Āyogava women. And their qualification is: "wearing dead clothes," which means they put on the garments of corpses. They are non-Aryans and untouchable. They eat food that is contemptible, such as leftovers, meat, and so forth. (10.35)
From a Niṣāda father and a Kārāvarī mother, a Carmakāra is born;
from a Vaidehika father, Andhra and Meda sons are born, whose dwellings are outside the village.

Because of the use of the restrictive particle *eva* in the subsequent passage, "He is born from a Vaideha woman alone" (MDh 10.37), there is an understanding here as well that "from a Niṣāda, one named Kārāvara is born from a Vaideha woman. From a Vaidehika [father], two types—the Āndhra and the Meda—are born. From which women? From the Kārāvarī and the Niṣādī, because of their proximity here. And since a different caste arises from a Vaideha father through a Vaideha mother, they are explained in this way. Due to the difference in the women, these two castes arise from a single caste; they are those whose dwelling and residence are outside the village. (10.36)
From a Caṇḍāla and a Vaidehī is born a Pāṇḍusopāka, who deals in bamboo; he is also called an Āhiṇḍika. (10.37)

From a Cāṇḍāla father and a Vaidehī mother is born the caste named Pāṇḍusopāka. His livelihood consists of dealing in *tvaksāra* (bamboo). *Tvaksāra* means bamboo; he lives by dealing in it—through the buying and selling of bamboo, or by making mats and such articles. From a Niṣāda father and the same mother is born the Ahiṇḍaka; his livelihood is this very same one, or it may be sought elsewhere. 10.37.
But from a Cāṇḍāla, by a Pulkasī woman, is born the sinful Sopāka, who subsists by the occupation of root-digging and is always censured by virtuous people. (10.38)

*Vyasana* means suffering; its root is killing, which constitutes their livelihood. Their mode of life consists of executing those condemned to death by royal decree, carrying the corpses of the destitute, seizing their clothes and other belongings, eating the funeral offerings (*pretapiṇḍa*) intended for them, and so forth. He is born from a *pulkasī* woman by a *caṇḍāla*. Alternatively, *mūla* refers to the roots of trees and such; their *vyasana* is the act of cutting them down, and that is their livelihood. When trees have been felled, they live by uprooting whatever root remains and selling it, and so on. (10.38)
But from a Caṇḍāla and a Niṣāda woman is born a son called Antyāvasāyin, who frequents cremation grounds and is despised even by those outside the caste system. (10.39)

They call the *antyāvasāyin* a *caṇḍāla*. Alternatively, one born from a *niṣāda* woman and a *caṇḍāla* has the name *antyāvasāyin*. He frequents the cremation ground, making his living by burning corpses and similar tasks; therefore, he should be understood as even more contemptible than a *caṇḍāla*. Thus, this has been provided merely as an illustration, for the mixtures (*saṃkara*) are infinite. (10.39)
These castes resulting from intermixture have been shown according to their fathers and mothers;
whether they are concealed or manifest, they are to be known by their own actions. (10.40)

Those occupations which were just mentioned—such as working with bamboo, trade, and so forth—are to be understood as belonging to those same classes even when they are not well-known by names such as *sopāka* and the like. They have been shown by both father and mother through their respective divisions. Whether hidden or manifest, they are to be understood as belonging to those same classes. Regarding *āyogava* women, the division was shown by the mother; regarding *niṣāda* and *vaidehika*, the division was shown by the father, resulting in the two sub-varieties of *āndhra*. (10.40)
Those born of women of the same caste and those born of intermediate castes are six sons who possess the dharma of the twice-born;
however, all those born of Śūdra women are remembered as being of degraded birth (apadhvaṃsaja) and possessing the same dharma as the Śūdras. || 10.41 ||

Those born from members of the three *varṇas* to women of the same caste possess the duties of the twice-born (*dvija*); this is merely restated as an established fact. The statement regarding the equality of those born in immediate succession is for the purpose of their acquiring those same duties. "Born in immediate succession" refers to those born in the natural order (*anuloma*): those born from a Brāhmaṇa to a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman, and those born from a Kṣatriya to a Vaiśya woman. The meaning is that they also possess the duties of the twice-born and are eligible for initiation (*upanayana*). Once initiated, they are entitled to all the duties of the twice-born.

But is it not the case that their status as belonging to the mother’s caste has already been stated [in Manu Smṛti 10.14]: “These [sons] belong to the caste of the mother immediately following [that of the father]”? And consequently, since they are equal to those [of that caste], their entitlement to the duties of that caste is indeed established.

True. Because of the mention of the term "immediate" (*anantara*) in the phrase "the immediate [son]," someone might suspect that this is merely a designation for them and not an extension of their caste status (*jāti*); therefore, for the sake of clarity, the statement begins with: "The six sons possess the duties of the twice-born. Furthermore, those born of degradation (*apadhvaṃsaja*), who are born of a mixture of castes (*saṃkaraja*), have the same duties as Śūdras; the meaning is that they are entitled to the same conduct and practices as those [Śūdras]. However, a specific distinction regarding those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*) will be stated later. The inclusion of the word "immediate" is intended to indicate the *anuloma* (direct) order. By this, even one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a Vaiśya mother—who is separated by one degree—is included. Because the number six is exceeded, the *pāraśava* born of a Śūdra mother is not included here. (10.41)
But by the power of the seeds of their asceticism, they undergo increase and decrease among human beings here, birth after birth, in age after age. (10.42)

These aforementioned offspring born in immediate succession, through the power of asceticism and the power of the seed, undergo increase and decrease in every age and in every birth; this we shall explain in the verse beginning, "Born from a Brāhmaṇa on a Śūdra woman" (MDh 10.64). 10.42.

This is an elaboration of what was stated [in MDh 10.24]: "by the abandonment of their own duties. But by the gradual omission of ritual acts, and by the transgression against Brahmins, these Kṣatriya castes have fallen to the status of Śūdras in this world. (10.43)

Where the omission of ritual acts (*kriyālopa*) is connected as something requiring purification (*saṃskāryatayā*), as in the case of the initiation ceremony (*upanayana*) and so forth; or where it is connected as the agent (*kartṛtayā*), as in the case of the obligatory *agnihotra* and twilight worship (*saṃdhyopāsana*) and so forth—the omission of these refers to the non-performance of both types. Consequently, the loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśa*) occurs not only through the absence of the initiatory rite, but also through the abandonment of the prescribed duties by those who have been initiated. Thus he says, "gradually" (*śanakaiḥ*). From the lineage of sons, grandsons, and so on, there arises the status of a Śūdra, but this does not apply to the person born [with that status] alone. In the absence of initiation, however, a different designation applies to him alone. Even though that birth-status (*jāti*) does not cease, for his sons and grandsons, another distinct caste such as *bhṛjjakaṇṭaka* becomes the basis for their designation. "By transgressing against Brāhmaṇas" means by transgressing the injunctions prescribed for Brāhmaṇas. Alternatively, it may mean the failure to approach the assembly (*pariṣad*) when there is doubt regarding the meaning of the scriptures or when a penance (*prāyaścitta*) is required. (10.43)
The Pauṇḍrakas, Auḍras, Draviḍas, Kāmbojas, Yavanas, Śakas, Pāradas, Pahlavas, Cīnas, Kirātas, Daradas, and Khaśas. (10.44)

Words such as *puṇḍra* and others are, in the ultimate sense, names of regions; however, here the view is adopted that they refer to the people of those regions because the principal inhabitants of those regions are Kṣatriyas. This is similar to the rule for the elision (*lup*) in Pāṇini 4.2.69, "His residence," and 4.2.81, "Elision when [the name refers to] a region," and not like the rule 1.2.54, "Elision because the connection [of the name] is not observed. The statement regarding their status as *vṛṣalas* is based on the fact that the four-fold caste system (*cāturvarṇya*) does not exist in abundance in these countries. Alternatively, if words such as *puṇḍra* are somehow seen apart from a connection to a region, then they should be understood as referring to this particular class of people. Since Kṣatriyas are described in the *Mahābhārata* and elsewhere, someone might have the misconception that even today these people are Kṣatriyas; therefore, it was said, "These are *vṛṣalas*. Furthermore, regarding those who dwell at the ends of the quarters—such as the Kirātas, Venas, Daradas, and others—the Veda reiterates what has not been previously established: "One should not go to the people, nor should one go to the ends. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 1.3.10). 10.44.

Those castes in the world who are outside those born from the mouth, arms, thighs, and feet—whether they speak the tongues of barbarians or the speech of the Aryans—are all remembered as Dasyus. 10.45.

Speech that consists of improper words whose meanings are non-existent is called *mleccha* (barbarian), such as that of the Śabaras, Kirātas, or other low-born peoples. Those who speak the *ārya* language and dwell in Āryāvarta are known as being of a different caste from the four-fold order (*cāturvarṇya*); at that time, they are called *dasyus* (outcasts). This is what is meant: residence in a particular region is not the cause of being considered barbarian speech; rather, it is the well-known usage of terms such as "barbarian" (*barbara*) and so forth as described above. The meaning is that those born of [low-caste] mothers are excluded from the categories designated by terms such as "Brāhmaṇa" and the like; all such people are called *dasyus*. (10.45)
Those who are considered the outcasts among the twice-born, as well as those born of degraded unions,
should subsist by means of those despised occupations of the twice-born themselves.

The *apasadās* (low-born) are those born in the natural order (*anuloma*) and those born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), as well as those born of illicit unions (*apadhvaṃsaja*); the distinction between them is like that between "cattle" and "bull. They should maintain themselves by performing services useful to the twice-born; because they perform censurable service, their occupations are censurable. (10.46)
And so it will be stated:
"The management of horses and charioteering for the Sūtas; medical practice for the Ambaṣṭhas;
service to women for the Vaidehakas; and the way of trade for the Māgadhas. (10.47)
Women’s work consists of guarding the inner apartments (*antaḥpura*). The merchant’s path is well known as consisting of land routes, water routes, and so forth. (10.47)
The killing of fish is the occupation of the Niṣādas, while that of the Āyogava is carpentry;
the Medas, Andhras, Cuñcus, and Madgus subsist by the slaughter of wild animals. (10.48)
Tvaṣṭṛ is the wood-cutter; his work is carpentry. || 10.48 ||
For the Kṣattrus, Ugras, and Pulkasas, however, there is dwelling in holes, as well as killing and binding;
for the Dhigvaṇas, the work of leather; and for the Veṇas, the playing of drums.

The *bilaukasas* are snakes, mongooses, cranes, and so forth; their killing and capture constitute the livelihood of the *kṣatras* and others. Leatherwork includes the sewing of armor and the like, as well as the stitching of sandals and so forth. The playing of musical instruments refers to drums such as the *muraja*, *ardhamuraja*, and others. (10.49)
These learned ones, subsisting by their own prescribed duties, should dwell at shrines, near trees, in cremation grounds, on mountains, and in groves. || 10.50 ||

Those living outside the village should dwell in regions characterized by mountains. Their caste marks (jāticihna) are known to the learned. Whatever occupation has been prescribed for each, by that alone shall he live; he is not permitted to perform superior work or engage in the mixing of castes (saṃkara). 10.50.
The dwellings of Caṇḍālas and Śvapacas shall be outside the village;
they must be provided with broken vessels, and their wealth shall consist of dogs and donkeys.

Their shelter and dwelling should be outside the village. They are *apapātra* (those excluded from using vessels), meaning that those who live with them for a long time must not clean the vessels in which they have eaten; rather, those vessels are to be discarded. This applies to vessels other than those made of gold and silver, for specific methods of purification for those two have been prescribed. Alternatively, the term may be *avapātra*: food such as parched grain (*saktu*) or boiled rice (*bhakta*) should not be given into their own attached vessels. Rather, having placed the food in a vessel resting on the ground or held by another's hand, they should take that vessel once it has been set down on the ground. Or, *avapātra* refers to a broken vessel, as he will say: "And eating from a broken utensil" (MDh 10.52), and so forth. Their wealth consists of dogs and donkeys; they should not accept cows, horses, gold, silver, or the like as property. (10.51)
His garments shall be the clothes of the dead, his food from broken vessels, and his ornament iron; this is the perpetual mode of life for a wandering mendicant.
Wandering should be undertaken at all times; they should not dwell in a single place. || 10.52 ||
A man practicing dharma should not seek association with them; their mutual dealings and marriages are only with their own equals. (10.53)

*Samaya* means a convention or a common purpose; *saṃgati* is a synonym. The meaning is that one should not engage with them in staying, sitting, or wandering in a single place. Marriage, such as taking a wife and so forth, is likewise prohibited in this very same way. 10.53.
Their food should be given by others in a broken vessel;
they must not wander at night through villages or cities.

That [gift] must not be given to them directly; it should be caused to be given by some servants in the manner previously described. There is a prohibition against wandering within villages or cities at night due to the danger of physical contact. 10.54.
They may wander about during the day for the sake of their business, marked by royal edicts; and they shall carry out a corpse that has no kinsmen—such is the established rule. 10.55.

They wander about during the day for the sake of business—namely, for the purpose of accomplishing their own tasks such as buying and selling—or they may go about for royal business, or on account of city festivals, spectacles, and the like. And even there, they are marked by royal edicts, distinguished by signs commanded by the king such as the thunderbolt and so forth, or by execution decrees, with axes, hatchets, and other implements carried upon their shoulders. (10.55)
And so it has been said:
"They shall constantly execute those condemned to death according to the scriptures by the king's command;
they shall take the garments, the beds, and the ornaments of the executed. (10.56)
One should discern by their own actions a man who is devoid of caste, unrecognizable, born of a defiled womb, and though appearing noble in form, is actually ignoble. (10.57)

Deprived of caste means fallen from the fourfold social order (*cāturvarṇya*). When there is suspicion, one who is unrecognizable—born of an adulterer—should be determined by the actions to be described and by his extraordinary natural traits. One who delights in base acts and performs cruel deeds, when such suspicion exists, should be known as born of a defiled womb, born of an adulterer. (10.57)
Lack of nobility, harshness, cruelty, and a lack of virtuous action reveal in this world that a man is born from a defiled womb. 10.58

The ignoble person is dominated by hatred and envy; he is harsh and intent on his own self-interest; he is cruel and devoted to greed and violence; he is inactive and shuns prescribed duties. By these characteristics, his birth from a defiled womb is revealed. (10.58)
He inherits the character of his father, or his mother, or indeed both; for one of base birth can by no means suppress his own innate nature. (10.59)
One of base birth, born of mixed parentage, does not invariably assume its own nature, that is, its inherent cause. 10.59
Even for one born into a preeminent family, if there should be a confusion of birth, that man will surely take on their character, whether to a small or a great extent. (10.60)
His lineage is that by which he was born, not that of his field; he is renowned in the world. 10.60
But in that country where these corrupters of the social orders are born through promiscuity, that kingdom, together with its inhabitants, perishes very quickly. (10.61)
Therefore, the king must avoid the intermixture of castes. The kingdom consists of the provincial inhabitants; the realm includes the ministers and others. 10.61

The unconditioned sacrifice of one's body for the sake of a Brahmin or for the sake of a cow, as well as for the protection of women and children, is the cause of success for those outside [the Vedic fold]. (10.62)

"Unadorned" means not having accepted wealth. "Favor" (*abhyavapatti*) means an act of grace. "Of outsiders" refers to those born into a lower caste. It is called a "cause of success" because it is the cause for the attainment of success through birth in a superior lineage; they obtain such a birth that they become eligible [for liberation]. Alternatively, "success" (*siddhi*) refers to the attainment of heaven and so forth. (10.62)
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, purity, and restraint of the senses—Manu declared this to be the summary of the dharma for the four castes. (10.63)

Purity (*śauca*) consists of external means such as earth and water. This summary has been stated for the entire class of *sarvamuṣya* [mixed castes] collectively, not according to the specific divisions of castes such as Brāhmaṇas and so forth. The rest has been explained. If non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) were the duty (*dharma*) of the *pratiloma* castes, how then was it stated: "Fishing is for the Niṣādas" (MDh 10.48), "killing and trapping burrow-dwelling animals" (MDh 10.49), and for those of Kṣatriya origin and others, "the killing of wild animals" (MDh 10.48)? And likewise: [141]

Some say: non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) consists in abstaining from those things which, for the sake of livelihood, have been declared as fit to be killed. Others think: for them, non-violence is a duty (*dharma*) because it is a means to achieve prosperity (*abhyudaya*); however, they do not accept that there is a prohibition against killing, just as in the case of the statement, "There is no fault in eating meat" (MDh 5.56). If non-violence is their duty, how then are they to live? If you argue that, due to some understanding [of scripture], the cessation of killing—which would otherwise be improper for them—is considered their duty, then what is their means of subsistence? Other modes of livelihood are restricted to specific castes. Teaching and the like are unattainable for them, being absolutely impossible. Agriculture and the like are restricted to Vaiśyas. For a Śūdra, there is service or some other common mode of livelihood. We shall demonstrate this under the rule, "Learning, craft... (MDh 10.116), showing how they might subsist. As for what is said, "They may subsist by the despised occupations of the twice-born alone," what could be more despised than killing? Furthermore, the slaughter of fish is not useful for the twice-born. Its utility occurs only occasionally at ancestral rites (*śrāddha*), when feeding guests, and so forth; it is not a constant source of livelihood. Therefore, killing and the like cannot be an independent means of subsistence. (10.63)
If one born of a Śūdra woman from a Brāhmaṇa father procreates with someone of a superior caste, he attains the higher caste within the seventh generation. (10.64)

In the expressions “he takes [her] in the womb” (*garbhe gṛhṇāti*) and “the embryo is born from hearing [the Veda]” (*garbhaś ca śravaṇāj jātaḥ*), the use of the masculine gender should be understood as referring to the offspring (*apatya*). Therefore, this is what is meant: if a maiden born of a Śūdra woman by a Brāhmaṇa is procreated by a superior Brāhmaṇa—one possessing excellence of caste—through a connection that serves as the cause for producing offspring sanctified by marriage and other rites; and if a maiden is born even of her, and she too is married by a Brāhmaṇa; and thus, through this succession, when the seventh generation is reached, he who is born there of a Brāhmaṇa woman attains [that status]. Although the term *śreyasā* (by a superior) refers generally to one of a higher caste, nevertheless, here, due to the proximity of the word *brāhmaṇa* and because of the subsequent statement, “The Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa” (MDh 10.65), it should be understood as the attainment of Brāhmaṇahood for the Śūdra class. By this same reasoning, for the caste born of a Vaiśya woman in the fifth generation, and for that born of a Kṣatriya woman in the third. Here too, there is an elevation from the female side. Thus, for a Vaiśya, the state of a Kṣatriya is attained in the third generation. For a maiden born of a Śūdra woman by union with another Vaiśya, the state of a Vaiśya arises in the third birth. For a Śūdra woman born of a Kṣatriya, it is in the fifth *yuga*. The word *yuga* denotes a birth. An inferior person—one of a lower caste—goes to or attains a superior caste. The prefix *ā-* is used in the sense of inclusion (*abhividhi*), meaning pervasively. (MDh 10.64)
A Śūdra attains the state of a Brāhmaṇa, and a Brāhmaṇa likewise falls to the state of a Śūdra; one should know that this is exactly the same for those born from a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya. 10.65.

The meaning has been stated: "A Śūdra attains the status of a Brāhmaṇa. And [the reverse is true]: "A Brāhmaṇa falls to the status of a Śūdra. Here, the "Brāhmaṇa" should be understood as a *pāraśava*, one born of a Brāhmaṇa father. If he marries a Śūdra woman possessing the aforementioned characteristics, then he incurs a degradation in birth; thus they explain it as the third [case]. As it has been stated, when a cycle of ages (*yugaparivarta*) has passed, those who have attained elevation are entitled to perform consecrations (*saṃskāra*) and ritual acts (*karman*). (10.65)
If one were to ask: "Wherein might there be superiority—between one born by chance from a Brāhmaṇa father and a non-noble mother, and one born from a non-noble father and a Brāhmaṇī mother? (10.66)

The word *kiṃ* is used in the sense of censure. If, due to the predominance of the seed (*bīja*), those born of women of lower caste gradually attain the status of the father's caste—surpassing that of the mother's caste—then this same principle should be observed even when the field (*kṣetra*) is predominant, as in the case of the *kṣetraja* son. Therefore, just as one born from a Brāhmaṇa father and a non-Aryan Śūdra mother becomes superior—even if she was not formally married to him by chance or in some other way—likewise, one born from a non-Aryan Śūdra father and a Brāhmaṇī mother attains excellence through the predominance of the field. As it has been said: "In some cases the seed [prevails], in others the womb" (MDh 9.34). || 10.66 ||

One born of a noble father from a non-noble woman may become noble through his qualities; but one born of a non-noble father from a noble woman is certainly non-noble—this is the settled rule. (10.67)

A son born to a noble man from a non-noble woman—one of low caste—would indeed be noble, provided she is of the Ārya class; that is, from a Brāhmaṇa of superior birth. But does this mean he possesses the actual status of the Brāhmaṇa caste? No, he says: "By virtue of qualities. That is, by way of a secondary application (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) based on qualities, merely through his eligibility for *pākayajña* and other such rites. He is called "noble" (*ārya*) in comparison to the [other] non-noble ones who will be mentioned later. A son born to a non-noble Śūdra from a noble Brāhmaṇa woman is certainly non-noble; this is the settled rule. What is meant is this: prominence rests solely upon what is explicitly stated in the text; it is not possible to infer anything else through logical presumption (*anumāna*). Therefore, union with a woman of the same caste is alone appropriate; the field’s predominance applies only to the *kṣetraja* son (the son born of the wife), and not elsewhere. 10.67.

And having established this, the Dharma is settled thus: both of these [the first and last castes] are not subject to refinement; because of the deficiency of their birth, the former is so by nature, while the latter is so by inverse order. (10.68)

Both the Caṇḍāla and the Pārāśava are unfit for the sacraments and ineligible for initiation. The explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) providing the reason for this is as follows: "The former [is so] because of the defectiveness of his birth. He who is born to a Brāhmaṇa from a Śūdra woman—despite the predominance of the seed—has a defective birth due to the fault of the womb. And the latter is the Caṇḍāla; he is born in the inverse order (*pratiloma*), and because of extreme inversion—even though the field (the mother) is predominant—he is so due to the fault of the father. (10.68)
Just as good seed sown in a fertile field comes to fruition, so too one born of a noble father from a noble mother is worthy of every refinement. 10.69

The two previously mentioned [castes] are not subject to sacramental rites (*saṃskāra*), whereas those born of their own species are subject to them; this is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) applicable to both cases. Therefore, this alone remains established, according to the teaching: "In some cases the seed, in some cases the womb" (MDh 9.34). However, marriage with a woman one degree removed [in lineage] is not proper. 10.69.
Some wise men praise the seed, others the field; still others praise both the seed and the field. In this matter, however, the established conclusion is as follows: (10.70)

Just as there are these three positions, and one or another position has been adopted by someone: some say that the seed alone is superior; thus, for example, one born from a Brāhmaṇa father in the three [lower] classes beginning with the Kṣatriya is superior by virtue of his mother's caste. Others, however, say: the field is best, because a *kṣetriya*—one born in whatever field—is of the same caste as that field, and his offspring belongs to that very [field]. Others consider both the seed and the field to be superior; as it is said: "Both a good seed and a good field" (MDh 10.69).
Not approving all of this, he said: "In this regard, however, the established position is as follows; this is what has been determined and settled here. (10.70)
Seed sown in a non-field perishes right there within;
and even a field without seed becomes merely a barren plot of ground. (10.71)

A seed sown even though cast into a non-field, such as saline soil (*ūṣara*), perishes within itself without having yielded its fruit. A field that is seedless or possesses unsuitable seeds becomes merely a barren plot (*sthaṇḍila*) or a wasteland (*khila*); the meaning is that no fruit is obtained from it. (10.71)
Since sages born of animal species became honored and praised through the power of their seed, therefore the seed is praised. 10.72.

Those who are honored by anyone are saluted; those who are praiseworthy are praised with words of eulogy. Therefore, they argue that the seed is superior—thus say the proponents of the primacy of the seed (*bījaprādhānyavādinaḥ*).
