This has been declared to be incorrect: "In this matter, however, the settled rule is as follows" (MDh 10.70). Alternatively, the phrase "by the power of the seed" does not demonstrate the primacy of the seed, but rather serves as a refutation. For one might suspect that because the seed is primary, Mandapāla and others—who were born from animals—were sages, since their status as sages is observed [in tradition]; yet in those cases, the sagehood of their offspring did not arise through the primacy of the seed, but rather through a specific quality of merit (*dharma*) produced by the power of austerity, sacred learning, and so forth. (10.72)
Having carefully considered the non-noble who performs noble deeds and the noble who performs non-noble deeds, the Creator declared: "They are neither equal nor unequal. (10.73)

The non-Aryan is a Śūdra. He is one who performs the duties of an Aryan, being devoted to service for the twice-born and the like, performing *pākayajña* sacrifices, and intent on bowing to the gods and the twice-born. The Aryan is a Brāhmaṇa or the other [higher castes]. He is one who performs non-Aryan acts, practicing what is forbidden and abandoning prescribed duties. Having thoroughly considered both of them and understood their respective qualities, the Creator Prajāpati Manu—having determined whether the superior quality belonged to one or if the final judgment lay with the other—declared: "They are not equal; even a Śūdra of excellent qualities would not be equal to one whose caste is more venerable. He spoke again: "Nor are they unequal; for what is the use of a high caste that is seized by many defects? This is what is meant: a person is not to be honored by relying on the power of caste, but rather qualities are to be honored. Caste is not able to protect one devoid of qualities, for that would lead to the absurdity of making the instruction on penance (*prāyaścitta*) useless. From the verse beginning with "born of a non-Aryan woman" (MDh 10.66) up to this verse, the purpose is to censure the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*) and to praise [proper] action. Nothing is here enjoined or prohibited, nor is any new matter made known as in a definition (*abhilakṣaṇavat*). Therefore, these verses are solely for the purpose of praise. 10.73.
Those Brahmins who abide in the source of Brahman and remain steadfast in their own duty should properly subsist by means of the six duties in their proper order.

An introduction to the duties in times of distress: their source is the cause. Brāhmaṇas established in the source of Brahman (the Veda) should subsist by, that is, perform, the six duties. Verbs have multiple meanings. [They should act] according to sequence and according to qualification—meaning, whichever person is qualified for whichever duty. Some [duties] are for the sake of spiritual injunctions, while others have visible purposes. (10.74)
Teaching, studying, performing sacrifices, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and accepting gifts—these six are the duties of the first-born (the Brāhmaṇa). 10.75.

In the first chapter, their recitation was for the purpose of praising the scripture; here, however, it is for the purpose of an injunction (*vidhi*). Although an injunction for them individually has already been stated, they are nevertheless mentioned here collectively out of kindness. This form [of the injunction] is indeed dependent upon other injunctions, as is the case with these ritual acts due to the specific scriptural statement (*vacana*). Therefore, having restated what has been prescribed, the matter about to be explained is enjoined. (10.75)
Of his six duties, however, three are his means of livelihood:
officiating at sacrifices, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from pure persons. (10.76)

The classification of the threefold action has a clear purpose. One set of three is adopted for a visible purpose by implication; the other has an invisible purpose. [One who is] "pure" is one whose actions are free from evil.
In this way, even a Śūdra may attain purity. What is your jealousy?

A contradiction with another Smṛti would result: "A Brāhmaṇa may eat and accept gifts from twice-born men who are eminent in their own duties" (GDh 17.1–2). If that is so, then it must be explained in such a way that no contradiction arises; for when non-contradiction is possible, contradiction is not logical.
Alternatively, this is merely a restatement (anuvāda), because this same matter has already been enjoined in such passages as "He should seek wealth from a king" (MDh 4.33). 10.76.
Three duties cease with respect to a Kṣatriya from a Brāhmaṇa:
teaching, officiating at sacrifices, and thirdly, the acceptance of gifts. (10.77)

These are not the livelihoods of a Kṣatriya; however, those acts which have an unseen purpose—such as sacrifice, study, and giving—are not prohibited. Furthermore, since the Veda is the subject under discussion, it is this teaching of the Veda that is forbidden, but not the science of archery, the arts, or the crafts. (10.77)
In the same way, these [duties] should cease with respect to the Vaiśya; such is the settled rule, for Manu Prajāpati did not prescribe those duties for them. 10.78.

This has been explained previously. These duties, such as teaching and so forth, were not stated by Manu Prajāpati for those two, the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya; the meaning is that they were not recorded [as their duties] in the Smṛti. (10.78)
The bearing of weapons and missiles is the livelihood of the Kṣatriya; trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are those of the Vaiśya. But the duty [of all] is giving, study, and sacrifice. (10.79)

This is their livelihood: *śastra* refers to weapons such as swords and the like; *astra* refers to the mantras associated with them, as established in the science of archery (*dhanurveda*). This [verse] is likewise merely a restatement of what has been said. The words "merchant" (*vaṇik*) and "livestock" (*paśu*) are employed here by including the specific activities within the general term: namely, trade (*vaṇijyā*) and cattle-rearing (*paśupālana*). Although the duties of Vedic study and so forth exist for all [classes], these [specific occupations] are predominant for them. (10.79)

The study of the Vedas is the specific duty of the Brahmin, protection for the Kṣatriya, and the occupation of trade and agriculture for the Vaiśya; these are their distinguished duties among their own respective tasks.

The study of the Vedas and teaching—these being derived from the section on livelihoods—are thus distinguished among one's own duties. Among the scriptural activities for livelihood, these are more conducive to spiritual welfare than other means of subsistence. (10.80)
But if he cannot subsist by his own prescribed duty as a Brahmin, he may live by the dharma of a Kshatriya, for that is the next best for him. (10.81)

When there is a depletion of his body, family, and obligatory duties, and he does not possess sufficient wealth for them, then he is said to be "not living" [ajīvan], by means of teaching and so forth as previously described. At that time, like a Kṣatriya, he may live by protecting villages and cities, by bearing weapons and missiles, and if possible, by exercising overall sovereignty. The root *jīv* has already been explained; it does not refer merely to the maintenance of the body. Rather, it also indicates the performance of the family's duties and the stability of obligatory rites, for that is his immediate concern. The term *pratyanantara* means "immediately following"; because it is stated as the cause, there is an exclusion of those who are separated [from this status], namely the evildoer. || 10.81 ||

Even when abandoning one's own livelihood, one should not think that there is no distinction in the transgression of the scriptures for Vaiśyas and Śūdras as well. Thus it is said: "If, unable to subsist by either [of these], one should ask how it may be, he may live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya, resorting to agriculture and cattle-rearing. (10.82)

"But if one cannot subsist by either of these two"—by this, the sequence is demonstrated: first the immediate mode of livelihood, and in its absence, the indirect one. The mention of agriculture and cattle-rearing is for the purpose of indicating the entire range of the Vaiśya’s livelihood; thus, he will later state regarding trade: "One may live by the livelihood of a Vaiśya. The relationship between an action and its means, characterized by the general and the particular, has been established previously.

In this regard, agriculture, trade, and usury are mentioned as permissible even when there is no distress, just like teaching and so forth. Some say: "Agriculture is remembered as being based on falsehood; trade, however, is based on both truth and falsehood" (MDh 4.5–6). It is also stated: "Agriculture and trade [are permitted] when not performed by oneself, as is usury" (GDh 9.5–6). Thus, performing these oneself is here expressly permitted.

As for the objection raised regarding the similarity [of agriculture] to teaching and other such activities, it has been refuted right here. If agriculture and the like were equally available to all, why would it be stated: "Trade, cattle-rearing, and agriculture are for the livelihood of the Vaiśya" (MDh 10.79)? It would not then be the case that these are not for the livelihood of the Brāhmaṇa and Kṣatriya either. Furthermore, in the verse: "Sacrificing for others, teaching, and the acceptance of gifts from the pure" (MDh 10.76), those [means of livelihood] would have been mentioned there as well. Therefore, for one who lives by the rules of teaching and so forth, agriculture and the like are indeed prohibited. As for the instruction of these [activities] elsewhere than in this specific context, its purpose has already been demonstrated in that very place. (10.82)
Even while living by the occupation of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa or even a Kṣatriya should carefully avoid agriculture, which consists mostly of violence and is dependent upon others. 10.83.

The censure of agriculture is for the purpose of praising the other occupations of the Vaiśya, and not for the purpose of prohibiting it; for if that were the case, the instruction regarding it would become meaningless. (10.83)
They consider agriculture to be an excellent thing, yet that livelihood is censured by the virtuous;
for the wooden plough with its iron-tipped mouth destroys the earth and the creatures dwelling within the earth. (10.84)

People consider agriculture to be a truly virtuous action (*sātkarma*). This is appropriate: for a man who plows, much grain arises; from that, he benefits guests and others by giving them food. Therefore, it is virtuous. And so it has been said: "One who is fond of guests does not thrive without plowing. "One should practice agriculture with effort, everywhere with diligence. Likewise: "The plowshare is wide-reaching, very auspicious, and well-handled; it draws forth the cow, the sheep, and the fat, swelling [cattle]" (TS 4.2.5.6), and so forth.

They do not think correctly, for that practice is censured by the virtuous. For what reason? "The plough with its iron-tipped wood destroys the earth. It also destroys those dwelling in the earth—those living beings such as grass-leeches and others that lie within the ground. [Objection: But what kind of destruction is there of the earth? For it does not experience pain from being struck by wood like a living being. [Reply: However, everyone has experienced the tearing up of the earth; this indicates that it possesses the same fault [of injury]. (10.84)
But for one who, due to a deficiency in livelihood, abandons skill in the Dharma, this may be sold as merchandise to increase wealth—provided that the choice pieces have been extracted. (10.85)

The word *idam* (this) is a reference to what is about to be stated. *Viṭpaṇyam* means the merchandise of the *viś* (the Vaiśyas); whatever is to be sold by Vaiśyas may also be sold by a Brāhmaṇa due to a deficiency in livelihood or a lack of wealth. Substances that are to be set aside are designated by the term *uddhāra*. That from which an *uddhāra* has been extracted is described in this way; meaning, having set aside the substances to be mentioned hereafter, the others may be sold. The phrase "for the increase of wealth" is a restatement of its inherent nature, for the increase of wealth is well known to result from trade. By the expression "skill in dharma" (*dharmanaipuṇa*)—which refers to steadfastness in dharma—he indicates that the sale of merchandise should not be performed [by one who possesses such skill]. From this it is understood: among all the occupations of the Vaiśya, agriculture is censured; trade is inferior to that; and cattle-rearing and so forth are inferior to those. (10.85)
One should exclude all liquids, prepared food along with sesame seeds, stones, salt, animals, and human beings. (10.86)

The six flavors, beginning with sweet (*madhura*), are prohibited when they constitute the primary quality of substances such as molasses, pomegranate, and *kirātatiktaka*. For it is impossible for flavors to exist in isolation. Although the word "flavor" (*rasa*) does not itself denote a substance through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*)—unlike words such as "white"—it nevertheless indicates the substance, just as in the expression "the hamlet on the Ganges. "He should avoid" means he should abandon; that is to say, he should not sell them. "Cooked food" refers to prepared food such as boiled rice (*odana*) and the like, but not raw rice grains (*taṇḍula*). Together with sesame seeds: sesame seeds themselves are also not to be sold. However, this is not a prohibition against sesame and cooked food when used together, nor is it a permission for them alone. "Stones" refers to all rocks. "Salt," even though it is not in the form of a stone, is included under the term "stone" in the case of rock-salt (*saindhava*). In the context of flavors, the mention of salt is for the sake of its constant prohibition; by this, the sale of sweet and other flavors is only optionally permitted. "Animals" includes both domestic and wild ones. "Humans" refers to human beings. (10.86)
And all woven cloth that is dyed, as well as hemp, linen, and wool—even if they should be undyed—as also fruits, roots, and medicinal herbs. (10.87)

*Tāntavam* refers to what is made of threads, such as garments, cloths, or large wraps (*bṛhatikā*). *Rakta* means red; the word *rakta* is more commonly established in the sense of the color red. For instance, even a white ox is called "red" (*lohita*). Although the meaning of the root *rañj* is also the imparting of another color to something white, [the rule applies] to linen, silk, and woolen cloth even when they are not red. As it says: "Even if they should be uncolored. The rest is well known. (10.87)
Water, weapons, poison, meat, Soma, and all kinds of perfumes; milk, honey, curd, clarified butter, oil, liquor, molasses, and Kuśa grass. (10.88)

*Śastra* refers to weapons such as swords, nooses, and the like. *Gandha* refers to specific substances such as *tagara*, *uśīra*, sandalwood, and so forth; this term is to be explained in the same manner as the word *rasa*. *Kṣīra* (milk), along with its derivatives, is well known from other *smṛtis* (cf. GDh 7.11). Therefore, even whey (*mastu*), coagulated milk (*kilāṭa*), buttermilk (*udaśvit*), and the like are not to be sold. The mention of curd (*dadhi*) and clarified butter (*ghṛta*) is included because of their preeminence. *Madhu* here refers to beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*), following the elision of a portion [of the compound], just as Devadatta is called simply "Datta. For that [selling of beeswax] is prohibited in another *smṛti*; furthermore, in this text, honey produced by bees (*sāragha*) is prohibited by the word *kṣaudra*, and *mādhvīka* (wine made from honey) is prohibited later under the category of intoxicants (*madya*).

Others, however, explain that the word *madhu* is used for the sake of prohibiting *mādhvīka* (honey-wine) while it has not yet reached the state of being intoxicating liquor (*madya*). That is incorrect; this term does not denote the juice extracted from crushed grapes. Rather, it exists as intoxicating liquor itself, as seen in the usage: “Both were intoxicated by honey-wine” (*madhvāsavakṣībau*, MBh 5.58.5), where intoxication is caused solely by liquor. Its mention is for the purpose of removing the prohibition against the juice of molasses (*guḍa*). Others, however, explain it as being for the purpose of permitting sugar-candy (*khaṇḍa*), granulated sugar (*matsyaṇḍikā*), and so forth. (10.88)
All wild animals, fanged beasts, and birds;
liquor, indigo, lac, and likewise all one-hoofed animals. (10.89)

The terms *āraṇyapaśu* (wild animals) and *śabda* (sounds/words) have been explained by the analogy of molasses and salt. This is for the purpose of permitting domestic animals; for even domestic animals are included under the prohibition regarding "connection with slaughter. *Daṃṣṭriṇaḥ* refers to fanged creatures such as dogs, pigs, and the like. *Vayāṃsi* refers to birds. *Ekaśaphāḥ* refers to single-hoofed animals such as horses, mules, donkeys, and so forth. Some read the word "many" (*bahūn*) in place of the word "likewise" (*tathā*); thus, there is no fault in selling a single one. (10.89)
Having personally undertaken agriculture and produced [the crop],
the farmer may sell pure sesame seeds for the sake of dharma, provided they have not been kept for long.

Regarding the rule, “cooked food together with sesame seeds” (MDh 10.86), there is an exception (*pratiprasava*) for those sesame seeds that were previously prohibited, based on their specific nature and purpose. “Pure” (*śuddhān*) and “not long kept” (*acirasthitān*) refer to the specific nature (*svarūpaviśeṣa*) of the seeds. “For the sake of *dharma*” (*dharmārtham*) refers to the specific purpose (*prayojanaviśeṣa*). “Pure” means unmixed with rice and other grains; for those mixed for the sake of *kṛśara* (rice-and-sesame porridge) and the like, sale is impossible. “Not long kept” means that one should not wait, disregarding profit such as wealth, thinking, “The price is low today, but in the future time I might obtain a high price. Alternatively, “pure” means non-black; black sesame seeds are prohibited. Or, the meaning of “not long kept” is this: what has been kept for a long time becomes black. Black seeds—whether produced by oneself or purchased—are not to be sold. The statement “a farmer [should sell] from his own cultivation” is a general restatement (*prāyiko ’nuvādaḥ*) and not intended to be taken literally. There is no prohibition even for those acquired through gifts and other means, provided they are sold for the purpose of *dharma*. Here, when cows are purchased with money for the sake of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and for the sake of Vedic study (*svādhyāya*), the *agnihotra*, and so forth; or when rice and other grains are purchased for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* and other sacrifices—that is sale for the sake of *dharma*. Likewise, if the sesame seeds themselves are used for *dharma* such as giving (*dāna*), or if they are used by the buyer for medicinal oil, that too is exactly the same. 10.90.
If one performs with sesame seeds any act other than giving them as food or as an ointment, he becomes a worm in dog dung and sinks there together with his ancestors. (10.91)
This is an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*) regarding the prohibition of selling sesame, intended to distinguish it from the sale of other types of sesame mentioned in the context.

Now, it was argued that the indication of a fault is connected as the very result of prohibitions; so why is this—"By doing with sesame anything other than eating, anointing, or giving, one becomes a worm"—considered an explanatory statement?

It is said: This is stated because of the hearing of an impossible result and one that is contradicted by other scriptures. For instance, it is said [in another text] that [one goes] "with the ancestors. Yet no wrong has been committed by them; for the fruit of good and evil deeds accrues to the agent, and it has already been stated previously that the ancestors can never be agents. Furthermore, regarding the statement "one falls immediately by [selling] meat" (MDh 10.92), there is a rule that the mention of "falling" (*patita*) for others does not imply their own state of being fallen. Therefore, the prohibition connects only with the fact that some undesirable consequence exists; it is not appropriate to take the text literally [as implying the ancestors themselves fall]. Wherever there is an act such as eating and so forth, and elsewhere—namely at places of sale and the like—whosoever deals with sesame seeds in such a manner becomes a worm and is joined with the aforementioned fault. (10.91)
One falls immediately from one's status by selling meat, lac, or salt;
by selling milk, a Brāhmaṇa becomes a Śūdra within three days. (10.92)
The meaning has been stated [in the previous verse]. || 10.92 ||
But by intentionally selling other types of merchandise here,
a Brāhmaṇa attains the status of a Vaiśya within seven nights.

From the expression "out of desire," it is inferred that this applies when there is no distress. The observation regarding the gravity or lightness of [the offenses involving] meat and so forth is for the purpose of specifying the particular penance; we shall explain that heavy [offenses require] heavy [penances] and light [offenses require] light ones (cf. MDh 11.58). || 10.93 ||
Flavors may be bartered for flavors, but salt must never be exchanged for flavors;
prepared food may be traded for unprepared food, sesame seeds for grain, and these are considered equal. (10.94)

The *rasas* (flavors) are those previously mentioned. They are to be bartered for other *rasas*. Having given sweet substances such as molasses (*guḍa*) and the like, one may take sour substances such as *āmalaka* and the like. One should not merely give salt and receive another flavor; however, there is an alternative reading: "salt with sesame seeds. In this reading, the prohibition regarding salt applies only to sesame seeds and not to other flavors. Prepared food (*kṛtānna*), such as groats or boiled rice, is to be bartered for cooked grain (*anna*), such as milk-rice (*pāyasa*) and the like. Sesame seeds, however, are equal to grain such as rice (*vrīhi*). Having given a *prastha*, one should receive exactly a *prastha*; one should not give more or less based on the market price. What is called "exchange" (*vinimaya*) is indeed a form of sale (*vikraya*). For the root *krī* (to buy) is listed among the terms for the exchange of goods. This is not correct, because while the context concerns sale, Gautama shows a distinction by stating, "but [this is] exchange" (*vinimayas tu*). If that is so, then "sale" is the handing over of goods for well-known currency such as coins (*rūpaka*), whereas "exchange" is the substitution of one substance for another. (10.94)
A Kṣatriya who has fallen into misfortune may live by all these means;
however, he must never at any time consider a higher mode of livelihood for himself.

By all this [it is meant]: this is a counter-exception (*pratiṣiddha-pratiprasava*) for the Kṣatriya regarding forbidden goods. Nothing whatsoever is prohibited from being sold by him, as it is for the Vaiśya; however, even if he must abandon his own livelihood, he should never think highly of the superior Brāhmaṇa-livelihood, nor should he form the thought in his mind, "I shall adopt this. Adverse fate is misfortune (*anaya*). This is intended to indicate times of distress (*āpad*). "Gataḥ" means arrived; that is to say, one who has fallen into distress (*āpad-gata*). 10.95.
If one who is base by birth should live by superior occupations out of greed, the king, having deprived him of his wealth, should banish him immediately. (10.96)

One who is lowest by birth and base—such as a Kṣatriya or others—even though the context specifically concerns a Rājanya, this prohibition against the Brāhmaṇa’s mode of livelihood applies to all. This verse is exactly so: the superior one is the Brāhmaṇa alone, independent [of others]. He lives by his duties, such as Vedic study and the like. He is to be punished with the confiscation of all property and banishment. (10.96)
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well-performed; for by living according to the duty of another, one falls immediately from one's caste. 10.97.

This is an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda) intended as a censure of the preceding injunction: that which is the duty prescribed for a person based on his birth may be performed even if it is deficient—that is, even if its constituent parts are incomplete—whereas the duty of another is not to be performed, even if it is complete in all its parts. Here, the censure is directed at the duty of another. (10.97)
A Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty may also live by the occupation of a Śūdra;
provided he does not perform forbidden acts and, being capable, he desists from them.

For a Vaiśya who cannot subsist by his own duty, the occupation of a Śūdra is permitted; that is, service such as washing the feet and so forth. Provided he does not perform improper acts—such as cleaning up food-leavings and the like, which are improper—he must avoid them. The phrase "if he is capable, he should desist" applies to all cases.

Regarding this, someone has said: "By implication, this is extended even to Brāhmaṇas and Kṣatriyas. To this, another objects: "How could a Brāhmaṇa engage in the occupation of a Śūdra? For it is heard in scripture [that he may not do so]."
"Superior and inferior occupations exist for those two;
having set aside the middle occupations, those two are indeed common to all.

This is incorrect. For its meaning is not that the occupation of a Śūdra is permitted for a Brāhmaṇa by implication. What then? It is as we have stated as a general rule [in verse 10.97]: "And one who is capable should desist [from the lower occupations]. [10.98]
But a Śūdra who is unable to perform service for the twice-born, having fallen into distress regarding his children and wife, may live by the work of artisans. (10.99)

Artisans are craftsmen, such as cooks, weavers, and so forth; their occupations, such as cooking and weaving, are well known. One should live by these. "Distress regarding son and wife" means the inability to support them. By this, it is inferred that these occupations are inferior, since marriage and other rites are prescribed for one in such adversity due to the failure of wealth and means. (10.99)
Those various crafts and diverse arts by which, when practiced, the twice-born are served— these are the works of artisans.

"By means of those practiced and performed. "They are served," meaning they are attended to. "Those activities and crafts" are those which are useful for that [service]. Although craft (*śilpa*) is indeed just the work of an artisan (*kārukarma*), nevertheless, because it is mentioned here separately, "artisans" refers to carpenters, builders, and so forth; their "works" are such things as carving and building; "crafts" refer to leaf-cutting, modeling, painting, and the like. (10.100)
A Brāhmaṇa who does not follow the occupation of a Vaiśya, yet remains on his own path, should practice this dharma when he is distressed by the lack of a livelihood and is suffering. 10.101.

"Without subsisting by his own choice"—this is what is meant: if, when the occupation of a Kṣatriya is impossible, he should practice the occupation of a Vaiśya or accept gifts from unworthy persons, these two occupations are equal; yet the occupation of a Kṣatriya is superior to accepting gifts from the unworthy. Or rather, "without subsisting by the occupation of a Vaiśya" [is said] when that too is impossible; consequently, accepting gifts from the unworthy is even lower than the occupation of a Vaiśya. By saying "standing on his own path," he indicates that there is a combination of these occupations in times of distress. "Emaciated by lack of livelihood" means suffering, reaching a state of exhaustion. (10.101)
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone; that the purifier should become defiled—this is not tenable according to the Dharma. 10.102

"In all cases" means that one should not take into account the specific caste or qualities of the recipient. For even here, among those who are inferior, more inferior, and most inferior, there is indeed a progression where, in the absence of each preceding category, the next succeeding one may be accepted—just as when the occupation of a Kṣatriya is unavailable, the occupation of a Vaiśya is permitted. The Ganges stream is pure; it is not defiled by contact with impurity, for it has been said: "A river is purified by its current" (MDh 5.107). In the same way, so too is a Brāhmaṇa. 10.102.
No fault attaches to Brahmins from teaching, from officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts—even from censurable ones—for they are like fire and water. 10.103

The acceptance of gifts from improper persons was mentioned previously; by this [verse], officiating at sacrifices and teaching are permitted. The phrase "from one who is censured" connects with the two preceding [activities] as well, according to the principle of the lion’s glance (*siṃhāvalokita*). This is a praise [intended to show]: "Just as fire and water are pure everywhere, so too are Brāhmaṇas."

Some say: "Neither sacrificing for the unworthy (*asadyājana*) nor teaching the unworthy (*asadadhyāpana*) are permitted in the same way that accepting gifts from the unworthy (*asatpratigraha*) is not. If they were [permitted], then they would have been recited in the previous verse alongside accepting gifts. However, here, because there is no optative suffix (*vidhipratyaya*), it follows that there is a fault for Brahmins. This is because, through the use of the present tense suffix, the statement is established as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). Furthermore, the mention of accepting gifts is itself an *arthavāda*, since it is already established by what precedes; and because they must form a single syntactical unit with that, sacrificing for the unworthy and teaching the unworthy ought to be understood in the same way."

We, however, say: even in that case, where the acceptance of gifts from unworthy persons is impossible, such conduct is appropriate; for it is recorded in the Smṛti as an engagement: "By whatever means possible, he should rescue himself, except from those things that entail sin. But the recitation of the rules for times of distress (*āpaddharma*) is intended for the sake of performing ritual acts. 10.103.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from here and there, is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud. (10.104)

In the preceding [verse], the acceptance of gifts from improper persons was forbidden; by this [verse], food that is tainted by such acceptance is permitted. The phrase "from here and there" refers to the owner of the food without regard for his caste or occupation. The remainder is a commendatory statement (arthavāda). 10.104.
Ajīgarta, driven by hunger, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.

There was a seer named Ajīgarta. Afflicted by hunger, he approached and prepared to kill his own son, named Śunaḥśepa. It is not fitting that he should be called a "meat-eater" (kravyāda). The narrative concerning Śunaḥśepa is well known in the *Bahvṛca* [Ṛgveda] (AitB 7.13). A detailed account of this scripture is not required here; rather, its ultimate meaning is an allegorical explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) whose nature is that of primordial matter (*prakṛti*). All such instances are to be understood in this way. 10.105.
Desiring to eat dog's flesh in his distress, Vāmadeva—who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma—was not defiled, for he did so for the sake of preserving his life. (10.106)
Thus there was a seer named Vāmadeva; afflicted by hunger, he desired to eat—that is, to consume—the flesh of a dog. || 10.106 ||
But the great ascetic Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger with his son in the lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.
The carpenter Vṛdha was not to be accepted as a gift; however, the seer named Bharadvāja then accepted many cows from him. || 10.107 ||
Afflicted by hunger, Viśvāmitra, who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla.

The great sage named Viśvāmitra was well-known. On a certain occasion, due to the suffering of hunger, he approached a dog’s haunch from the hand of a *caṇḍāla* with the intent to eat it, having resolved upon it. The mention of the "dog’s haunch" implies that there is a fault not only in food that is defiled by external circumstances, but also in that which is defiled by its very nature. The intended meaning of the verse is that even food defiled by every kind of fault may be eaten in times of distress. (10.108)
Whether from receiving gifts, officiating at sacrifices, or likewise from teaching, the acceptance of gifts is the lowest of these for a Brahmin and is censured after death. (10.109)

The meaning of the verse is that when the possibility of officiating at sacrifices or teaching exists—even if these involve slight censure—then one should not engage in accepting gifts from censurable persons during times of distress. (10.109)
Sacrificing for others and teaching are always performed by those who have been consecrated;
however, the acceptance of gifts may be performed even from a Śūdra of the lowest birth. 10.110

In this very context, there is an explanatory statement (arthavāda) in the form of a reason: such is the conduct of the world that those who have not been initiated do not study nor perform sacrifices. Therefore, even when in great distress, one will not officiate at a sacrifice for a Śūdra or teach him. Giving, however, is well known to be permitted for all castes; thus, it follows that one may accept gifts even from a Śūdra. Consequently, [officiating at his sacrifice or teaching him] is inferior. (10.110)

Sin committed through officiating at sacrifices or teaching is removed by recitation and burnt offerings; however, that caused by receiving gifts is removed only by renunciation and austerity. (10.111)

Through recitation (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*), sin departs and is destroyed; therefore, there is no harm [to the recipient]. As for the sin arising from the acceptance of a gift, that is removed by the renunciation of that gift and by austerity (*tapas*) as will be described: "Having drunk milk in a cow-pen for a month," and so forth (MDh 11.193). || 10.111 ||
A Brahmin who cannot subsist otherwise may gather grains from anywhere;
gleaning ears of corn is better than receiving gifts, and picking up individual grains is praised even more than that. (10.112)

This explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) expresses a mere commendatory passage (*arthavāda*). It is a great injustice to seize the property of another; yet, even if one occasionally seizes what is not heard of [as permitted], this [act] becomes praiseworthy for one who is otherwise blameworthy by such a means. Here, *śila* (gleaning) belongs to the same class as *pratigraha* (acceptance of gifts). This very [act of gleaning] serves as the cause for the suffix of excellence (*prakarṣapratyaya*), [expressing]: "Gleaning is better than acceptance of gifts. For excellence is experienced as a cause of superiority in relation to something inferior. Indeed, it is not the case that a Brahmin is superior to a Caṇḍāla. Therefore, even when taking *śila* and *uñcha*, there is no seizing of what is not one's own. Nevertheless, *śila-uñcha* is better. Even though the livelihood of *śila-uñcha* is said to be absolutely superior, there is still some similarity between it and acceptance of gifts. Because in that [latter case], there is a deficiency in ritual action resulting from the presence of deities presiding over it or from the arrival of servants [of the donor]. In the case of accepting improper gifts (*asatpratigraha*), the seizing within oneself is justified, thinking, "He will not be provoked to anger. In that context, the seizing within oneself refers to property situated elsewhere. Therefore, even the livelihood of *śila-uñcha* is not entirely blameless. Thus, it is logical that "gleaning is better than acceptance of gifts," and so forth. (10.112)
A lord of the earth should be entreated by *snātaka* Brahmins who are sinking into distress and desiring base metals or wealth; if he is unwilling to give, he deserves to be abandoned. (10.113)

In this context, three grounds for accepting gifts from a king are stated. "By those sinking" means by those who have reached the ruin of their household or are in distress. "Desiring base metal" refers to earrings, bracelets, and the like; turbans, seats, and so forth; gold and other wealth such as cattle or bullion; or anything else suitable for sacrifice. Brahmins [218] may beg from a lord of the earth; a ruler of a region should be entreated. Regarding this, what was stated—"One should not accept gifts from a king" (MDh 4.84)—that prohibition should be understood as referring to a wicked king. Thus it has been said: "From one who is greedy and acts contrary to the scriptures" (MDh 4.87). One who, when asked, does not wish to give because he is unwilling to part with his property, deserves to be abandoned; one should not dwell in his domain. Alternatively, "abandonment" (tyāga) means loss. Since no other [consequence] is specified, one incurs a loss of dharma. 10.113.

From a field where grain has been sown, one may take unprepared grain; likewise, from among cattle, goats, sheep, gold, grain, and food, each preceding item is free from blame compared to the one following it.

A field that is unplowed and uncultivated is praiseworthy; so too is a flock of goats and sheep. The meaning of the verse is understood as expressing a mutual distinction between these things. 10.114.
There are seven righteous means of acquiring wealth: inheritance, gain, purchase, victory, investment, professional labor, and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous. 10.115

*Āya* is wealth inherited through lineage. *Lābha* is the acquisition of buried treasure and the like, or a share from property acquired by a father or other relative. Although such [property] has come down through the succession of one's father and others, it nevertheless cannot be designated by the term *dāya*, because it is common to many [relatives]. Thus, it is stated in another Smṛti: "A fixed endowment is *dravya*" (YDh 2.124). Alternatively, that which is obtained out of affection from a friend or from the house of a father-in-law is *lābha*. *Kraya* (purchase) is well known. *Jaya* (conquest) occurs in battle. *Prayoga-karma-yogāḥ* refers to usury, agriculture, and trade. And thus, these are lawful according to the distinction of social classes (*varṇa*). Among them, the first three are common to all; conquest belongs to the Kṣatriya; usury, agriculture, and trade belong to the Vaiśya; and the acceptance of gifts from the virtuous is the specific [means] for the Brāhmaṇa. Even among all classes, the rule of partition is as previously shown.
Some dispute over the purchase price; that is not correct, because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the collapse of all commercial transactions.
Some even desire that victory [in a legal case] be determined by a wager on every subject matter.
That is incorrect, because in other *smṛtis*—specifically in the passage "pārśvikadyūta" (NSm 1.43)—it is stated that wealth acquired through gambling is impure (*aśuddhi*).
Furthermore, others say that *prayoga* means non-activity (*avyāpāra*). For instance, the usage "jñānapūrvaprayogaḥ" is observed; in that context, it is understood as the employment of words.
Likewise, there is the expression "karmaprayoga," meaning the performance or practice of an action. (10.155)
Learning, craftsmanship, wages, service, cattle-rearing, trade, agriculture, contentment, begging, and usury—these are the ten means of livelihood. 10.116.

This mode of livelihood is permitted for all men in times of distress. In this regard, knowledge—excluding the Vedic sciences—such as the sciences of medicine, logic, elemental spirits, and the neutralization of poisons, is not blameworthy when pursued by anyone for the sake of subsistence. Artisanal craft has already been explained. Wages consist of servitude. Service is the following of another’s occupation. Contentment is *dhṛti*. This is stated for the sake of illustration; therefore, these means of subsistence may be intermingled according to the state of one's prescribed livelihood, since they pertain to all men alike. (10.116)
Neither a Brāhmaṇa nor even a Kṣatriya should ever practice usury;
however, for the sake of dharma, one may at will give a small amount to a more sinful person.

"For the sake of dharma" should be understood as referring to the aforementioned course of action in times of distress. Because of the expression "from one who is more sinful," not even a small amount should be accepted from a righteous person. As for what was said—that "agriculture, trade, and usury are equal to teaching"—that refers to one who has fallen into distress. (10.117)
Even when taking a fourth part as his share in times of distress, a Kṣatriya who protects his subjects to the best of his ability is released from sin. || 10.118 ||

For a king whose treasury is depleted, an exception to the rule of taking a sixth part is permitted, and a fourth part is authorized. The remainder is a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). The word "param" is an adverbial modifier, meaning "by means of supreme protection. (10.118)
Victory belongs to him who follows his own duty; he must not turn his back in battle.
Having protected the Vaiśyas with his weapon, he may collect the lawful tribute.

By the word "victory" (vijaya), that which is joined with the fruit of victory is prescribed as his own duty (*svadharma*). Thus, he should not turn his back in battle; the meaning is that when fear has arisen, he should not turn away from the fight. Having protected the subjects in this manner, the tax (*bali*) must be collected from the Vaiśyas. Since Vaiśyas possess great wealth, those appointed to collect it in such a way are not killed even if they have committed an offense. (10.119)
The toll on grain for the Vaiśyas shall be one-eighth; for other goods, it shall be one-twentieth, with a minimum of one kārṣāpaṇa.
Śūdras who provide labor, as well as artisans and craftsmen, [shall pay this].

An eighth part of the profit of those who trade in grain should be taken. The word *viṭ* signifies the subjects (*prajā*). Of those who trade in gold, a twentieth part [should be taken]. Śūdras are those whose service is their means of subsistence; since their service is their instrument of livelihood, they should not be made to pay anything at all. The same applies to artisans and craftsmen. This was stated previously in the verse beginning with "Artisans [shall pay] month by month" (MDh 7.139). This present verse is intended for the purpose of prescribing a larger share [of profit]. 10.120.
But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, may serve a Kṣatriya;
or, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, a Śūdra may seek his subsistence.

But a Śūdra, desiring a livelihood, should then serve a Kṣatriya; because he is taking up service for the sake of subsistence, this service to a Kṣatriya is solely for the purpose of a livelihood, not for the sake of dharma. It is implied that service to a Brāhmaṇa serves both purposes. In this manner, having served a wealthy Vaiśya, he may live. (10.121)
For the sake of heaven, or for the sake of both, he should propitiate the Brahmins;
for one who has acquired the title of "Brahmin," that indeed constitutes the fulfillment of his purpose.

"It should be propitiated"—this is what is meant. He says that: when the designation "Brāhmaṇa" has arisen for him—that is, when this term "this is a Brāhmaṇa" applies to him—then he should be known as one who has accomplished his duty and achieved his purpose. Alternatively, it may be explained as "one for whom the designation 'born as a Brāhmaṇa' has arisen"; that is, when the designation "this person is dependent upon the Brāhmaṇas" arises for him. (10.122)
Service to the Brahmins alone is proclaimed as the distinguished duty of the Śūdra;
for whatever else he performs becomes fruitless for him. (10.123)

Service to Brāhmaṇas alone is the primary duty of a Śūdra. Whatever else he performs, such as vows, fasts, and so forth, that is fruitless for him. However, there is no prohibition against his performing acts such as giving gifts or the *pākayajña* sacrifices, because these are explicitly ordained for him. The prohibition of other [duties] is intended as a praise of service to Brāhmaṇas. (10.123)
He should provide for his livelihood from his own family estate as is appropriate, having regard for their capacity, their skill, and the number of dependents they maintain. (10.124)

This is the duty of the twice-born. A means of livelihood must be provided for him while he performs service. He should be protected like a son from one's own family; considering one's own capacity and his own skill in performing tasks, one should provide maintenance for all, taking into account the number of servants, children, wives, and dependents belonging to him who are to be supported. (10.124)
Leftover food should be given, as well as worn-out garments, the dregs of grain, and old household utensils. (10.125)

The meaning of the word *ucchiṣṭa* has already been explained. That which remains after guests and others have eaten should be given to a Śūdra who is dependent on him. Likewise, worn-out clothes that have been washed and turned white; likewise, *pulāka* grains, which are seeds lacking substance; and likewise, household furnishings such as beds, seats, and so forth. (10.126)
A Śūdra incurs no sin whatsoever, nor is he entitled to sacramental rites;
he has no obligation regarding dharma, yet there is no prohibition against him from dharma. (10.126)

This entire verse is a restatement (*anuvāda*). That which has not been specifically prohibited for him by way of direct mention—such as violence, theft, and so forth, which are prohibited by general rules (*sāmānya-śāstra*) without regard for specific caste distinctions—the transgression of these does not produce sin for him. However, that which is explicitly heard by the word [of the scripture], such as violence, theft, and so forth, in those cases he certainly incurs fault. Nor is he eligible for the sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*) characterized by initiation (*upanayana*). As it has been said: "The three castes are the twice-born" (MDh 10.4). Thus, he has no entitlement to religious duty (*dharma*), such as ritual bathing, fasting, or the worship of deities; he has no obligatory entitlement (*nitya-adhikāra*) to them. By their non-performance, he does not incur sin. There is no prohibition from dharma in the sense that there is no sin in failing to perform those acts of bathing, fasting, vows, and so forth for which there is no obligatory entitlement, provided there is no specific prohibition. If there is no such prohibition for him, then because they are not prohibited by the learned (*śiṣṭa*), it is appropriate for one desiring prosperity (*abhyudaya*) to practice them. Likewise, his abstention from eating garlic and similar things should be understood as being for the sake of prosperity, since it is enjoined by the general rule: "Abstention, however, yields great fruit" (MDh 5.56). Therefore, the argument begins with the statement: "there is no prohibition from dharma. (10.126)

But those who desire dharma, who know dharma, and who practice the dharma of the virtuous, do not incur blame when [performing acts] excluding the use of mantras; rather, they receive praise. (10.127)

This very point he states: those who desire to attain the Dharma and seek higher prosperity (abhyudaya), having practiced and relied upon the Dharma of the virtuous and the wise, do not incur fault—provided they exclude the mantras. Therefore, those who practice the conduct of the virtuous, such as fasting for many days, worshipping deities, and prostrating to gurus and Brahmins, do not incur fault; rather, they obtain praise and its fruit.

Furthermore, one must not think: "Those rites of the Brāhmaṇas and others, such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and so forth, which are accompanied by mantras—these do not incur fault for a Śūdra if performed excluding the mantras. For, when rites have been prescribed as being accompanied by mantras, their performance without mantras would be non-scriptural (*aśābda*). The scope of the phrase "excluding the mantras" has thus been demonstrated. And so the venerable Vyāsa said: "It is certain that a Śūdra does not fall [from his status] here, nor is he entitled to the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) here."

"But one who is engaged in [only] what is prescribed by Smṛti does not partake of Dharma, nor is there any prohibition of Dharma for him recorded in Smṛti. This too is merely a restatement of what has been previously ordained. One does not fall [from caste] due to the consumption of garlic, liquor, and the like; rather, it is simply stated that such a person is unfit for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). And it has been said that because he is uninitiated (*anupanīta*), in the absence of Dharmas prescribed by Śruti, those Dharmas generally ordained in the domain of Smṛti according to the aforementioned methods are not prohibited for him. Accordingly, another Smṛti states: "He should himself perform sacrifices with *pākayajñas*; the *namaskāra* formula is permitted as his mantra" (GDh 10.64–65).

Furthermore, as for those who say that Śūdras have an optional entitlement to the establishment of the domestic fire (āvasathya), the pārvaṇa rites, the vaiśvadeva, the pākayajñas involving cooked food, and so forth—

We do not understand their intention. First of all, the establishment of the domestic fire (*āvasathyādhāna*) has been prescribed by the authors of the *Gṛhyasūtras* specifically for the members of the three [upper] castes; it has not been so prescribed by Manu and others. Likewise, it is not prescribed there at all that "one should perform the domestic rites in the marriage fire" (*vaivāhikāgnau kurvīta gṛhyaṃ karma*, MDh 3.57). How, then, could there be an establishment of the fire for a Śūdra? If it is argued that the establishment of the fire is implied by the prescription of the *pākayajñas*, that too is not the case; the *vaiśvadeva* rite will take place in the ordinary worldly fire (*laukikāgni*). What is explicitly stated in the text is authoritative, and nothing else is capable of being implied. This has already been demonstrated in the discussion on the phrase "in the marriage fire. Furthermore, if by the word *pārvaṇa* the *āmāvāsya* (new-moon) *śrāddha* is meant, we grant that; for the *aṣṭakā*, the *pārvaṇa-śrāddha*, and the *vaiśvadeva* have been enjoined [for the Śūdra]. If, however, the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are intended, that has already been refuted. (10.127)
For in whatever measure one who is free from malice abides in virtuous conduct, in that same measure he, being blameless, attains both this world and the world beyond. (10.128)
The meaning of this verse has already been explained. || 10.128 ||
For even a capable Śūdra should not engage in the accumulation of wealth;
for a Śūdra, having acquired wealth, oppresses the Brāhmaṇas themselves. (10.129)

Even if capable, a Śūdra must not accumulate wealth through activities such as agriculture. Regarding this, he states an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) concerning the nature of the reason: "Having acquired—that is, having taken possession of—much wealth, a Śūdra oppresses the Brāhmaṇas alone.
But what constitutes the oppression of the Brāhmaṇas?

Because of his great wealth, he might excessively cause Brāhmaṇas to accept gifts from him; yet the acceptance of gifts from Śūdras is forbidden for them. By becoming the occasion for such an act, he would incur sin. Furthermore, there is no suspicion of ritual fault in one who performs what is not prescribed. Therefore, "he should not serve Brāhmaṇas"—this alone is the prohibition. (10.129)
These duties for times of distress have been proclaimed for the four castes;
by performing them correctly, they attain the supreme goal. 10.130

By the correct performance of duties during times of distress, the supreme goal is attained. Since there is no transgression of prescribed rules when protecting one's body, the attainment of auspicious results is logical. This is a restatement of the principle of the scriptures: that one who has fallen into distress need not hesitate regarding the acceptance of improper gifts and the like. 10.130.
This entire rule of dharma for the four castes has been proclaimed;
hereafter, I shall declare the auspicious rule for penance.
This is established by the mere recitation [of the text]. || 10.131 ||
Thus ends the tenth chapter in the Mānava Dharmaśāstra, in the Saṃhitā proclaimed by Bhṛgu.

The *Manusmṛti* is venerable, and Medhātithi’s commentary upon it is indeed appropriate; yet, by the power of fate, that [commentary] has vanished, such that no manuscript of it can be found anywhere.
Therefore, King Madana, together with his son Araṇasuta, had a restoration of the worn-out text prepared from manuscripts brought from various regions and transcribed here and there.
Thus [ends the work] composed by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Bhaṭṭa Vīrasvāmin.
The tenth chapter in the Manu-bhāṣya.
